items.text:
Auth output owns or borrows bytes until its handshake write completes, then the
runtime releases them. Exchange.Close always runs, including aborted handshakes;
Success runs only after AUTH_SUCCESS. Metadata internal queries obey context
bounds and new codecs. Unix sockets use Dialer and protocol 3 explicitly. Cloud
configuration is a builder for Config/TLSForHost/dial hooks; it retains SNI
UUID, per-host routing and ticket-cache verification without old query
interfaces. Pool sizing validates nonnegative ConnectionsPerHost and
ConnectionsPerShard. DefaultConfig sets host count 0 and shard count 1. Positive
ConnectionsPerHost selects per-host mode even when the shard count remains
positive; otherwise a positive ConnectionsPerShard is required. Both zero is
invalid. Per-host mode targets that total count across shards and disables
targeted shard-port filling, but retains token/shard-aware selection among
available connections. Per-shard mode targets its count separately on each
discovered shard (one for nonsharded hosts). MaxExcessPerShard is nonnegative;
zero retains no excess connections. MaxRequestsPerConnection is in 1..32,768
(default 32,768), including all native nonnegative stream IDs.
SourcePortStart..SourcePortEnd is an inclusive nonempty range within
1,024..65,535 when shard-aware dialing is enabled; defaults are 49,152..65,535.
An exhausted or unrepresentable shard-specific port search fails explicitly and
uses the documented ordinary-port fallback; no helper panic is permitted.
Initializing/ready/broken/closed are distinct pool states; closed is terminal
and cannot schedule refills. Endpoint/reshard generations fence late opening
attempts so they cannot reinstall superseded endpoint/sharder state. The same
fence covers route, proxy, SNI and TLS-target generations; late successful
handshakes for old targets are closed rather than published. Reconnect uses
bounded exponential backoff with jitter, independently of startup timeout. Host
filtering applies before query pool acquisition; bootstrap/control contact
exceptions are documented explicitly.

items.text:
All user hooks/providers/policies/logger/observers are invoked without driver
locks and must support the documented shared concurrency. Synchronous callbacks
(HostFilter, timestamp generator, policy methods, observer/logger/lifecycle
calls) must return promptly, perform no blocking I/O and must not synchronously
call blocking Session.Close, Bound.Wait or other operations that wait on their
own execution. Schedule such work separately. Context-taking
DNS/dial/translation, TLSForHost and auth hooks must honor cancellation. The
driver cannot preempt arbitrary caller code; its deadline/drain promises assume
these callback contracts. Observer/logger panics are contained and diagnosed
without corrupting execution.

items.text:
ClientRoutes requires nonempty unique connection IDs and nonempty override
hostnames for configured IDs only. Use the first configured available route and
keep it sticky while valid; deletion selects the next configured available ID.
DNS/connect failure may try remaining configured route IDs for that same host
under the same deadline, without changing unrelated hosts. Missing required
routes/ports fail explicitly; there is no fallback to the advertised direct
address. Route reads/partial deletions obey per-pair generation fences.
Combining client routes with a user AddressTranslator or enabled shard-aware
source-port dialing is invalid; the cloud/client-route builder disables the
latter explicitly. TLS routes require usable verified TLS and logical SNI;
setting the route flag alone never supplies trust configuration. Config
snapshots copy route IDs and override maps.

the stated Go contract rather than claim Rust already guarantees the stricter
behavior.

accepted predecessor's work. Shared signature changes update both artifacts and
notify affected owners before implementation. Intermediate compilation may
contain old private runtime implementations; release completion requires
removing the public compatibility surface and all old hot-path calls.

custom-codec/policy costs and explicit public copies separately; neither can be
used to hide built-in overhead.

section: gocql v2 implementation and acceptance contract
items.text:
Named Unix contacts and strict local-only behavior follow the API's transport
setup section. Bootstrap placeholders remain private; broad discovery-disabled
identity reconciliation still belongs to step 05. Context-aware hooks select raw
endpoints first and apply TLS exactly once. Defensive snapshots clone mutable
TLS containers/DER/OCSP/SCT buffers, while immutable parsed trust certificates,
private keys, provider callbacks and session caches keep shared obligations.
Positive CoalesceWait is supported for typed TLS by ordered span writes under
one writer serialization boundary, without driver plaintext assembly. Valid
requested compression must be advertised by the server; typed setup rejects an
unsupported algorithm before STARTUP instead of silently running raw. Raw TCP
wrappers must expose requested socket-control methods or fail explicitly; cloud
SOCKS IO wrappers forward those methods to their actual raw socket.

section: gocql v2 implementation and acceptance contract
items.text:
Typed pools separate membership from sizing: positive per-host count caps the
total and avoids targeted filling; otherwise counts/pending dials are maintained
per actual shard. Per-shard excess is bounded by that shard's configured count,
including zero. Endpoints and sharder revisions fence late successes, including
incompatible initial opens before a typed picker was installed. Typed repair
triggers after errors or acquisition use the configured policy/backoff; startup's
first fill is distinct. A stop decision cannot be bypassed by a later query.
Normal requests use another free eligible connection or await a reserved slot
under their context; strict host/shard targeting is preserved and no extra slot
is manufactured.

items.text:
The current transport-only incremental seam is exclusiveConn.exchange plus
streamResponse/decodeStreamRow. exchange installs receive ownership before
writing, returns checked metadata/row count before row payload, and owns the
page context used for every row read. There is no extra per-row context API.
Reservation-lifetime cancellation is registered once; a distinct page context
has at most one watcher, invalidated under a generation gate at exact completion.
Canceled generations cannot close a later page or a reused shared connection.
No per-row AfterFunc/scheduler allocation is permitted. Runtime step 07 must
compose these seams with admission, prepared fences, metadata plans, paging and
public RunStream; it must merge session/request lifetimes and join its cursor
registry on shutdown.

items.text:
Reader handoff acknowledges complete frame/v5-segment boundaries, finishes a
partial header/event, and never transfers unread buffered unit bytes. Native
v5 retains one bounded verified arena. Reusable release consumes only legitimate
control frames already in that final unit, without waiting for another socket
unit; malformed leftovers poison the connection. Close clears both unit storage
and interface-held data slices, and response release drops reader/body/control
references. Caller-owned output remains independent.

items.text:

record, releases them after consumption or terminal drain, and rejects terminal

streaming connection. Conn.waitEventDispatch is the tracked join seam for the
broader step 05/07 session lifecycle; this step does not claim all existing
metadata/control worker shutdown paths have been reconciled.

Driver configuration reporting, runtime capacity and metrics support all
32,768 nonnegative native stream IDs exactly. The reporting schema accepts
positive integers; the earlier inferred32,767 schema cap was disproven by
inspection and removed. Advertised shard counts are checked nonzero16-bit
values, IDs are below that count, and ignored MSBs are0..63 (explicit0 is valid).

targets retain their requested size while opening at most32 connections at a
time, stopping a failed batch for policy-governed repair.

application-defined representation and application-provided payload storage.

cell in a driver buffer. Read eligible uncompressed payloads directly into
their final caller-provided byte ranges. Parse fixed scalars with bounded
scratch and assign decoded Go values to the destination fields.

items.text:
The caller exclusively lends the destination and its writable payload ranges
during NextInto. The decoder may write only within those ranges and must not
retain pointers after that call completes. It never accesses caller storage
from prefetch workers or unrelated requests. No background payload receive into
that storage is permitted between calls. Caller-owned output survives cursor
and session closure; reusing the same arrays may overwrite previous output.

response completion and restored protocol boundaries; do not return a partially
consumed connection to the pool.

history remain covered by their separate ProtocolLimits budgets. v3/v4 raw and v5 raw/LZ4 with optional TLS are required initial modes;

one configured pool capacity unit, atomically quiesces/hands off shared I/O and
is held across pull-driven pages. Return requires exact framing and acknowledged
shared-reader resumption; failure/early close discards the connection.

section: Routing, replicas, tablets, and lightweight transactions
items.text:
Routing chooses an ordered sequence of coordinator nodes and shard hints for a
request. It combines statement routing metadata, an immutable cluster snapshot,
replica placement, location preference, connection availability, and optional
latency history. Token and tablet awareness reduce forwarding; deterministic LWT
routing reduces Paxos contention; leader awareness reduces forwarding for globally
consistent tablet keyspaces. These optimizations do not change the request's
consistency or make an otherwise invalid CQL operation valid.

items.text:
- Plain-session unpaged and manually paged unprepared requests have no token/table
  in their load-balancing input. Supplying bind values makes execution prepare on
  the chosen connection and can compute a tablet-version hint, but does not
  retroactively rebuild that request's plan or turn it into a token-aware plan.
  Automatic paging differs: an unprepared call with nonempty bind values is fully
  prepared through the session before entering the prepared pager, so token-aware
  planning and the table's partitioner are available. With empty values it keeps
  the token-unaware native QUERY path.

- A plan retains one metadata snapshot and the initial routing input. Retry
  changes to consistency do not recompute it. The retained nodes have live pools:
  connection availability and advertised sharding information may change while
  the plan is consumed. Shared policy latency state can change independently too.
  Snapshot ownership therefore preserves topology/tablet data, not an atomic
  observation of all target eligibility and shard hints. An empty plan ends
  execution without a coordinator; it is not an instruction to ignore the policy
  and choose any known node.

Failure to obtain a connection for a target advances directly to the next target
without consulting the retry policy or issuing a load-balancing success/failure
callback. When an attempt returns an error, its failure callback precedes the
retry decision; ignoring a write error therefore still reports that failed attempt.
Same-target retries reacquire a connection for the same node/shard hint, while next-target
retries consume the existing plan. Within an execution fiber, exhausting a
nonempty plan returns the last connection-selection or attempt error; an initially
empty overall plan yields the distinct empty-plan error. These paths do not refresh
routing metadata or restart the plan.

A custom policy supplies a cheap optional first target and an on-demand fallback
iterator over node/optional-shard pairs. Fallback is requested when first choice
returns nothing, when execution needs another target, or when speculation needs
one. Returning no first choice is therefore different from returning an empty
complete plan. Policies receive the routing input and cluster snapshot and can
observe successful/failed attempts with node and elapsed time; failure callbacks
also receive the attempt error. Shared policies must support concurrent use.
The interface does not automatically wrap a custom policy with the default
policy's host, location, LWT, leader, or latency behavior.

Groups with no candidates are omitted. In particular, an eligible remote replica
precedes a local non-replica. Replica groups are shuffled for ordinary requests.
Connected non-replica node groups are cyclic traversals with a newly random
starting offset, not a persistent counter or a full random permutation. The fast
node choice uses that rotation even for its final enabled-node stages; the first
acceptable node after the offset need not be uniformly distributed over a sparse
filtered subset. The full fallback's final enabled-node groups instead retain the
locator's stored unique-node order, which follows first occurrence from the
lowest token in the corresponding ring.

latency partition is not reordered again as statistics change.

beyond its remaining elements exhausts it. The ordered iterator is not cloneable.

the negotiated Scylla LWT metadata extension and are absent on Cassandra.

items.text:
When choosing across all datacenters, the fast LWT path inspects the first ordered
replica only. If it exists but fails the predicate, the operation returns no fast
choice and deliberately delegates to the full fallback; it does not skip to a
random node or claim the plan is empty. The full fallback computes and filters
the remaining ordered replicas. Datacenter/rack-scoped selection can cheaply find
the first matching replica directly. Global NTS ordering computes the primary
without allocation and materializes the remaining ordered replica set only when
needed. Explicit latency penalties may move otherwise preferred LWT replicas
later; LWT routing is not insulated from that configuration.

- The generic deserializers impose weaker byte-consumption checks than a strict
  payload validator. A null replica list is accepted as empty; in V1, omitting
  the final replica-list field entirely has the same effect. V2 still requires
  its non-null version field. Trailing bytes after the expected outer tuple or
  replica tuple fields, and bytes beyond a replica list's declared element count,
  are ignored. Thus an undeclared malformed tail need not reject feedback, and
  an accepted null/omitted list can replace usable cached replicas with an empty
  mapping. These are implementation quirks, not recommended server encodings.

- On a V2 connection every EXECUTE includes a one-byte version block. For a
  known version, select a random nibble index 0–15, put the index in the high
  nibble and that version nibble in the low nibble, numbering from the least
  significant nibble. A cache miss with table/token uses a random byte. With no
  table/token, use zero. The connection's negotiated feature controls whether
  the byte is written, independently of how the hint was computed. A request can
  reuse its chosen hint on retries; the random probing guarantee is across
  successive requests, not a required resample on every wire attempt.

items.text:
- EXECUTE responses, including the response after automatic repreparation,
  forward feedback when prepared table identity is available. This happens before
  interpreting a database error, including the initial UNPREPARED response, so a
  failed query can still update the cache. A transport/body decoding failure that
  prevents a response from being returned cannot reach this feedback step.
  Feedback is sent through a bounded channel of 8,192 entries with an awaited
  send, so a full channel can delay return from execution. A closed receiver is
  ignored by the sender. This is not an unbounded, nonblocking telemetry queue.
  Enqueueing does not wait for snapshot publication. Cancellation while the send
  is pending can discard that feedback; once enqueued, it can still be applied
  after the request times out or loses a speculative race. Thus neither a wire
  response nor a successful query return guarantees that a subsequent snapshot
  already contains its feedback.

- The cluster worker batches available feedback and publishes an updated cluster
  snapshot. Identical range/version/ordered node-shard data is a no-op only when
  all replicas are resolved. Updates within a batch are compared with the state
  produced by earlier entries in the same batch. A repeated unresolved mapping
  can still trigger work. No version ordering rejects older in-flight feedback.
  Metadata and tablet updates are applied serially by the same cluster worker,
  but feedback carries table names, not a schema generation or table ID. Late
  feedback can recreate a removed cache entry after schema maintenance or apply
  to a newly recreated table with the same name; maintenance is reconciliation,
  not a fence against such feedback.

The leader must be connected and eligible under the datacenter restriction. A
remote leader outranks a local-rack replica only if remote nodes are permitted.
The fast choice also rejects a latency-penalized leader. The full fallback first
promotes an eligible connected leader, then applies the stable latency partition
to the entire plan: a penalized leader moves behind unpenalized targets but stays
first among penalized targets. If the leader is unknown, disconnected, excluded,
or prohibited by the datacenter restriction, normal replica routing remains
available. The remaining replicas retain ordinary or LWT ordering before latency
partitioning.

items.text:
- Shard-aware source ports map by `source_port mod shard_count`. The default
  candidate range is inclusive 49,152–65,535; custom ranges must be nonempty and
  within 1,024–65,535. Candidate iteration begins randomly and wraps through each
  compatible port once. A valid range can have no port for a given shard, even the
  default range when the shard count is large. The iterator is then empty; the
  public single-port draw helper panics instead. Source-port helpers also assert
  that the requested shard is below the advertised count.
  The advertised count is a nonzero 16-bit number (1–65,535). Parsing rejects
  missing/empty shard parameters, zero shard count, parse errors, and shard IDs
  outside the advertised count. See connections for handling these errors during
  startup.

items.text:
Latency statistics are per host ID, shared by all requests using the policy, not
per shard. Successful attempts and designated failure classes update an average;
zero-duration measurements do not change it. The previous average's weight is
`ln(1+d)/d`, where `d` is elapsed time divided by scale, and is one when elapsed
time is nonpositive. Invalid floating-point duration conversion keeps the previous
average value while advancing its timestamp and measurement count. Defaults are
threshold 2, minimum 50 measurements, scale 100 ms, global-minimum refresh interval
100 ms, and retry period 10 s. A zero scale is rejected by a panic in the Rust builder.
The measurement minimum and retry period accept zero: a zero minimum still needs
an actual nonzero-duration sample to create an average, and a zero retry period
prevents penalties. The exclusion threshold has no positivity or finiteness check;
the comparison below uses the supplied floating-point value directly.
The periodic minimum updater belongs to the policy instance, so sharing one
policy shares its samples and updater across sessions/profiles as well as requests.

items.text:
A host is penalized only when it has enough measurements, its last measurement is
younger than the retry period, and its average is **strictly greater** than the
threshold times the last computed global minimum. Comparisons use microsecond
precision. Unknown hosts or absent minimum data are eligible. Periodic minimum
calculation considers hosts with enough measurements and does not itself expire
old averages. Penalty expiration gives the host another chance without deleting
its history. Statistics are keyed by host ID; the implementation has no explicit
"reset on node restart" hook despite that claim in a builder comment.

The fast connected-candidate stages reject penalized hosts. If all such choices
fail, the final enabled-node stages can still select one. The fallback stably
partitions the entire default plan into unpenalized and penalized targets, so
penalties may move a replica behind a non-replica or a preferred-local host behind
a permitted remote host. They never admit a host excluded from the underlying
plan.

items.text:
Driver-side serialization failures, broken connections, stream-ID exhaustion,
and fast server errors (bootstrapping, unavailable, unprepared, overloaded, and
rate limiting) do not update latency. Result/error/body-extension parse errors,
unexpected responses, repreparation identity errors, unfinished-page errors, and
the enumerated remaining server errors do. Unrecognized numeric server error
codes become `DbError::Other` and do update latency; only additional enum variants
not covered by the explicit match are excluded. This classification is an explicit
policy, not measurement of whether each failure physically involved a replica
round-trip.

Host filtering controls whether a node gets pools and is distinct from locality
preference. Built-ins accept all peers, accept one datacenter, or accept resolved
allowlisted socket addresses. The allowlist accepts untranslatable addresses
(contact points or already-accepted translated nodes); it compares translatable
peer addresses against the configured set. A custom filter can disable every
usable node and thereby produce empty default plans.

items.text:
- Connection-local preparation constructs a statement with the default Murmur3
  partitioner ([constructor](https://github.com/scylladb/scylla-rust-driver/blob/f8b0ee928dc0dcb475247dc82cce4e42804b0621/scylla/src/statement/prepared.rs#L248),
  [connection preparation](https://github.com/scylladb/scylla-rust-driver/blob/f8b0ee928dc0dcb475247dc82cce4e42804b0621/scylla/src/network/connection.rs#L763)).
  Only session preparation replaces it from table metadata
  ([assignment](https://github.com/scylladb/scylla-rust-driver/blob/f8b0ee928dc0dcb475247dc82cce4e42804b0621/scylla/src/client/session.rs#L2018)).
  Consequently, an unpaged/manually paged unprepared call with bind values can
  compute its tablet hint using Murmur3 even for a CDC table. Its plan is already
  token-unaware; do not infer CDC-correct hint selection from this path's local
  preparation alone. Automatic paging with values uses session preparation and
  therefore does select the table's partitioner.
  Session partitioner lookup searches the base-table map only, not the
  materialized-view map; preparing a view therefore retains the default even if
  its view schema has a partitioner override ([lookup](https://github.com/scylladb/scylla-rust-driver/blob/f8b0ee928dc0dcb475247dc82cce4e42804b0621/scylla/src/client/session.rs#L2027)).

items.text:
- Building a policy with latency awareness spawns its periodic updater through
  Tokio, so construction requires an active runtime. Dropping the last owner of
  the policy drops its remote handle and cancels the updater. Unlike zero scale, a zero update
  rate is not rejected by its setter: the spawned updater's timer construction
  panics when polled. The remote handle is retained without being awaited, so
  this failure is not returned as a policy-construction error. It is not a
  supported way to disable updates ([updater construction](https://github.com/scylladb/scylla-rust-driver/blob/f8b0ee928dc0dcb475247dc82cce4e42804b0621/scylla/src/policies/load_balancing/default.rs#L3439),
  [unchecked setter](https://github.com/scylladb/scylla-rust-driver/blob/f8b0ee928dc0dcb475247dc82cce4e42804b0621/scylla/src/policies/load_balancing/default.rs#L3760)).

Migrate the existing gocql routing, policy, tablet, shard-aware-port, batch/LWT,
and control integration scenarios to the new API without weakening assertions.

items.disposition: Go uses canonical encoded bindings, explicit policy Plan/Next and tri-state conditional safety; unknown partitioners disable token routing; no Rust caching-wrapper or all-host preparation API is required. Leader/tablet/latency behavior remains required and has actual current assertions.

Same canonical signed-byte/composite hash and captured Murmur3/CDC/custom partitioner; unknown names do not use a fabricated hash.
Exact host/shard sizing and pending/excess capacity, checked source/NAT fallback, endpoint/sharder/closed-state fences and repair-policy delay/stop.
Lazy host-specific preparation, cancellation, immutable routing schema/dependency identity and no warm global LRU/compile serialization.
Actual bytes-written/server evidence governs safe/downgrading retry; unknown/conditional statements cannot speculate, timestamps and inputs remain canonical.
Private publication-time indices and lazy locality/fallback with no full-host first lookup, deterministic LWT, explicit eligibility and strict pins.

items.text:
Use exact token boundaries, minimum/maximum token values, empty rings, many vnodes
per host, multiple racks including missing names, unknown datacenters, zero and
oversized replication factors, mixed-shard duplicate hosts, and a preferred rack
with no live replicas. Include confirmed and unconfirmed serial reads, batches
whose first statement is unprepared and later statements are LWT, changed retry
consistency, and exhausted first-choice filters. Distinguish a disconnected node
from a disabled one. Compare unprepared automatic paging with unpaged/manual
calls, including key-calculation errors and CDC partitioner selection. Separate
connection-acquisition failures from attempt failures when checking callbacks.

section: Routing, replicas, tablets, and lightweight transactions
items.text:
For tablets exercise cold caches, contiguous versus overlapping ranges, splits and
merges, unknown leaders versus followers, materialized views, out-of-order feedback,
V1-only/V2/mixed connections, repeated identical updates, late feedback after schema
changes, and more than 64 replicas in datacenter masks. Check V2 probing with a
controlled random source rather than assuming a finite probabilistic convergence
bound. Distinguish malformed declared replicas from ignored trailing bytes;
include null/omitted lists, empty-list replacement, and feedback on failed
EXECUTEs. Test channel saturation and snapshot lifetime separately from
routing correctness, including cancellation before enqueue, publication after
enqueue, feedback arriving after table recreation, and automatic paging over a
concurrently replaced mapping. Pause between plan advances to change pool/sharder
state, and distinguish shared iterator advancement from concurrent attempts.
For latency, control time and measurements; cover equality at the
threshold, penalty expiration, zero samples, stale global minima, and all-targets
penalized behavior.

items.disposition: Go retains pool/shard/reconnect/keepalive capabilities with explicit checked controls. Stable request identity covers queued cancellation; effective orphan capacity is enforced. Concurrent session USE propagation is deliberately replaced by initial/qualified/v5 per-request keyspace. Rust unbounded queues, ignored cancellation races and identity-only diagnostics are not copied as defects.

confirmed_claims: Historical staging/process description does not assert that the old private filename or Rust limitation is a current API. Carried-forward behavior is checked through the exact normative API confirmations and final matrix.

It strengthens queued cancellation, all-orphan/effective capacity, identity/deadline/source-port checks and explicit socket errors; Rust unbounded notifications, age-only orphan holes and keyspace fanout races are not adopted.

items.text:
A session maintains a pool for each enabled node, multiplexes requests over each
connection, and replaces failed connections asynchronously. The pool can target a
connection count per node or per shard. Requests prefer their target shard but can
use another live shard on the same node when its pool is incomplete. This is a
description of Rust revision `f8b0ee928dc0dcb475247dc82cce4e42804b0621`, not a proposed
Go contract. Node selection belongs to [routing](routing.md); control-connection
selection and topology handling belong to [metadata and events](metadata-control-events.md).

items.text:
These defaults come from session configuration. The low-level connection defaults
compiled for tests disable CQL keepalive and must not be confused with session
defaults. The configurable reconnect-policy API is unstable and gated by both a
build configuration flag and a feature; the default policy is also used when that
public customization is unavailable.
Session creation rejects a zero CQL keepalive interval. It does not reject zero
connect or CQL keepalive timeouts; zero is a timeout value, not a disable switch.
CQL keepalive is disabled by an absent interval, and its timeout is disabled by
an absent timeout. Pool counts and the millisecond coalescing delay use nonzero
values.

items.text:
4. Send OPTIONS and parse SUPPORTED. Discover sharding information, the TLS or
   plaintext shard-aware port appropriate to this connection, optional host ID,
   compression capabilities, and protocol extensions. Sharding parser errors
   cause operation without sharding information: the three required fields must
   have first values that parse as a 16-bit shard ID, a nonzero 16-bit shard count,
   and an 8-bit ignored-MSB count, and the shard ID must be below the shard count.
   The ignored-MSB count has no additional range validation here; values 64–255
   are accepted by discovery. Malformed optional host IDs are logged and treated
   as absent. Only the shard-port key matching the connection's TLS mode is
   inspected, and only its first string is parsed as an unsigned 16-bit port
   (including zero). An absent, empty, or invalid matching entry does not fall
   back to the opposite TLS/plaintext key or a later string.

items.text:
The connect timeout is not restarted around a single umbrella operation covering
all seven steps. Address translation, TLS, OPTIONS, authentication, STARTUP, and
REGISTER have no such common deadline inside the open-connection routine.
Cancellation by an owning layer can still terminate an attempt. CQL keepalive
starts only after TLS and router construction, so it cannot bound address
translation or TLS. A keepalive failure can fail a pending CQL setup request,
but it does not impose a deadline on an authenticator's asynchronous callbacks.

fallback does not rewrite the session configuration or other connections.

items.text:
Disabled nodes have no pool, never open data connections, report disconnected,
and return a host-filter-disabled error on connection selection. Pool-refill and
keepalive hints on such a node are no-ops. An address-only change preserves the
pool when the node remains enabled and its host ID, datacenter, and rack remain
unchanged, and updates the endpoint used by future connection attempts. Existing
connections and already-started attempts are not synchronously replaced. If the
refreshed node is enabled, a datacenter/rack change or enabling a previously
disabled node instead creates a new pool. A transition to disabled creates a
node without a pool. Retained older node handles can still
own their earlier pools, as detailed in
[metadata snapshot publication](metadata-control-events.md#merging-and-publishing-snapshots).

items.text:
The public ScyllaDB-detection accessor returns an unknown value when the node has
no Ready pool. Otherwise it examines the first connection in the published pool
(the first nonempty shard bucket in a sharded pool). It returns true if that
connection has valid sharding information, a parsed matching-mode shard-aware
port, a parsed LWT metadata mask or rate-limit error code, tablet-routing v1/v2
support, or metadata-ID support; otherwise it returns false. A host ID alone is
not a detection signal. This observes one connection's negotiated features, not
an independently verified product identity or agreement among all connections.
The control connection uses its own detection result for ScyllaDB-only metadata
timeouts and their configuration report, as described in
[metadata and events](metadata-control-events.md) and
[configuration and security](configuration-security-observability.md).

items.text:
For a non-sharded pool, choose one existing connection uniformly; a one-element
pool bypasses random-number generation. For a sharded pool with a requested shard,
first choose uniformly among that shard's connections. If the requested shard is
empty or outside the discovered shard range, visit all shards in a random
permutation until a nonempty shard is found and select a random connection there.
An externally supplied shard number too large for 16 bits is diagnosed and
converted to shard zero before this selection. A representable but out-of-range
shard is diagnosed and takes the fallback path.

items.text:
Without a requested shard, first draw a shard uniformly, then use the same
selection/fallback algorithm. This describes the pool's random-connection helper.
Ordinary session execution instead resolves an absent policy shard hint in the
routing plan, using the node's then-observed shard count or shard zero without
sharding information, and subsequently calls the pool with that explicit hint.
The plan's observation and the pool selection can therefore use different
snapshots. Neither random choice is weighted by the number of connections
per shard. Selection is independent of in-flight request counts and does not
reserve stream capacity. A selected connection can therefore reject a request
because it has no stream IDs even when another connection has capacity. Cross-node
retry or fallback remains the execution layer's responsibility. Failure to obtain
a connection skips directly to the next plan target without consulting the retry
policy; stream exhaustion after selection is an attempt error and does consult
that policy, as described in [execution](execution.md#request-attempt-deadline-and-error-boundaries).

items.text:
A new fill is scheduled only when the pool is under target and the previous
batch of connection/setup futures is finished. At that scheduling decision, a
clear failure flag resets the nominal backoff to 50 ms; a flag set by any
ordinary-port or keyspace-setup failure doubles it, up to 10 s. A batch that leaves
the pool full does not itself invoke either outcome callback. Each scheduled
delay gets independent jitter and is clamped. Thus the first failed immediate
fill normally schedules a nominal 100 ms delay. Dropping
below target after a connection failure does not itself set the batch-failure
flag; the next scheduling decision uses the current flag. Refill is persistent,
with no fixed retry-count limit, provided the pending attempts finish. A stalled
translation, TLS handshake, authentication callback, or unanswered CQL setup
request can leave a batch pending indefinitely. In the last case this can happen
with keepalive disabled, or while keepalive responses continue to arrive. Such a
pending attempt prevents a new refill batch even if the active pool later becomes
empty; a refill hint does not cancel or replace it.

items.text:
A reconnect-policy factory is called once per pool, and that pool retains the
returned mutable policy session. A custom implementation can still share state
internally; the driver does not enforce isolation between those sessions.
Its successful-fill/fill-error callbacks are invoked when scheduling a
needed refill, according to the failure flag, rather than once for every completed
batch. A refill hint also invokes successful-fill immediately, even if no refill
is needed; scheduling after that hint can invoke it again. The built-in exponential
policy permits custom minimum and maximum delays, requiring minimum no greater
than maximum. Its jitter range must be nonempty and start at a nonnegative
multiplier. The alternative constant policy multiplies its fixed duration by
the same default jitter range, without exponential growth or clamping; its
success/error callbacks leave the duration unchanged. A multiplier range of
exactly one disables jitter. These customization contracts do not promise that
invalid floating-point configurations outside the explicit checks are accepted
or normalized.

items.text:
Ordinary-port connections landing on an already-full shard are retained as excess
connections, excluded from request selection, while later fills seek missing
shards. Their failures are monitored, but existing excess connections are never
promoted when an active connection fails. Losing the last active connection can
therefore publish Broken while live excess connections remain, even on a shard
that now lacks capacity; recovery opens new connections. Excess connections are
also excluded from keyspace-switch snapshots and immediate keepalive hints.
The excess list is cleared when its size
exceeds ten times the shard count, or once the active pool is full. Per-host mode
has an excess limit of zero. A targeted connection that cannot be accepted causes
an immediate ordinary-port replacement attempt and is discarded, rather than
being retained as excess. Resharding discards both active and excess collections
and creates buckets for the newly discovered shard configuration before accepting
the new connection. Here a configuration change includes a change in shard count
or ignored-MSB count, and either gaining or losing valid sharding information;
loss of that information creates one non-sharded bucket. These changes occur only
after the new connection's keyspace setup succeeds. Each such completed
connection also replaces the pool's advertised shard port, even if it is later
classified as excess; a missing port clears the previous value. References
already held by requests can outlive removal from the pool; publication is not
synchronous cancellation of those users.

Any failure while opening a targeted shard-port connection starts an ordinary-port
attempt immediately. A subsequent keyspace-setup failure instead follows the
ordinary failed-fill handling described above. The opening failure alone does not
mark the fill unsuccessful or increase
backoff: the ordinary port might work, and multiple successful ordinary-port fills
can be necessary to cover all shards. The port used in a targeted endpoint is
set before address translation, so translation must preserve the intended
reachability semantics.

items.text:
If a successful targeted connection reports a different shard while reporting
the same sharding configuration used to calculate its source port, suspend
advanced shard awareness for that node for 300 seconds. This commonly indicates
source-port rewriting. Already-in-flight attempts can still finish. Further
mismatches during the suspension do not extend its deadline. A mismatch explained
by changed shard configuration does not cause this suspension, even if the pool
has already adopted that new configuration from another attempt. After the
deadline, later fills may use the shard port again; expiration alone does not
replace a full pool. A mismatched connection may still be accepted into its actual
shard when that shard needs capacity. Token/shard routing remains available while
advanced connection establishment is suspended.

items.text:
Each connection has a bounded submission queue with capacity 1024. A request is
serialized before queue submission and assigned a per-connection 64-bit request
identity distinct from its eventual wire stream ID. Its counter starts at zero
and wraps modulo 2^64 without a wrap guard, so identities repeat after 2^64
allocations on that connection. Queue submission
waits when full; the queue limit is not an overall bound on already-serialized
requests held by waiting callers. The writer allocates a free nonnegative 16-bit
stream ID immediately before writing. All 32768 IDs, including zero and 32767,
are usable; allocation chooses the lowest currently free ID. Exhaustion returns
a stream-allocation error for that request without
writing it; it does not wait for a free stream and does not by itself close the
connection. Keepalive shares this stream space: if its OPTIONS request encounters
exhaustion, the keepalive failure closes the connection as described below.

items.text:
The writer consumes queued requests and writes their serialized frames through
an 8192-byte buffer. When the queue becomes empty it either flushes immediately,
yields once to the scheduler, or waits the configured positive millisecond delay
and checks again. The delay occurs on an observed empty queue, not before every
request and not as a fixed latency guarantee. Buffered writes may flush earlier
when capacity requires it. The reader also has an 8192-byte buffer. Coalescing
does not change request identities or response association.

items.text:
Responses can arrive out of order. A nonnegative stream ID releases its stream
slot and is dispatched to its waiting request, or discarded if the request was
marked orphaned. An unsolicited nonnegative stream breaks the connection.
Stream minus one is treated as a server event only when an event receiver is
configured; otherwise it is ignored. Other negative streams are ignored. This
filtering happens after reading the whole frame: invalid direction/version or
an unknown response opcode still breaks the connection, and an incomplete body
can stall the reader even on a stream that would be ignored. An ignored frame's
body is not decompressed or deserialized. Event
decoding failures, unexpected event responses, or failure to deliver to the event
receiver break the connection. Event delivery awaits a bounded receiver, so
event backpressure can stall that connection's reader.

items.text:
Cancelling a request's response future sends its request identity to an unbounded
orphan-notification channel. If it still maps to an allocated stream, remove its
response handler and record the stream's orphaning time while keeping the stream
reserved. A later response frees the slot and removes the orphan record without
delivering data to another request. With distinct request identities, normal
response processing removes the request-to-stream mapping, so a late cancellation
notification cannot orphan a
new request that reused that stream ID. Notifications with no current mapping
are ignored; the implementation does not retain pre-allocation cancellation
notifications or promise that queued cancelled work is never transmitted.
If a notification is processed before the writer allocates that queued request's
stream, the writer can subsequently allocate and send it without an orphan
record. Its handler and stream then remain until a response or router termination,
and the old-orphan counter below does not count it. Cancellation alone therefore
does not guarantee that every abandoned request enters orphan-age tracking.

items.text:
Once per second the router counts streams orphaned for approximately at least
one second. If that count is greater than 1024, it closes the connection with a
too-many-orphaned-streams error. Exactly 1024 does not trigger closure; young
orphans and old orphans below the count threshold are tolerated. The age uses
time of orphan notification processing, not original request submission time.
This is a recovery mechanism for stuck requests, not server-side cancellation.

items.text:
Connection and pool background-task lifetime is tied to retained handles. Dropping
the last pool handle cancels its refiller; closure of the keyspace request channel
also terminates the worker when that branch can be polled. Dropping a connection
cancels its router when no connection owner remains. Removing a connection from
a published pool does not revoke other retained references, and there is no
graceful-drain promise in these internal connection/pool APIs.

items.text:
CQL keepalive begins after the first configured interval, not immediately at
router start. Missed ticks use delay behavior rather than burst catch-up.
An immediate keepalive hint wakes a connection's keepalive loop, sends OPTIONS,
and resets the next periodic interval. Hints received during an in-progress
keepalive retain a wakeup for the next iteration; multiple unconsumed hints can
coalesce. A pool forwards the hint to every currently published connection.
When CQL keepalive is disabled, hints do not create an active keepalive loop.

items.text:
If the keepalive request fails or its configured timeout expires, the router
breaks the connection. The timeout covers queue submission and waiting for the
raw response, so a congested submission queue can consume it before OPTIONS is
written. Without a timeout it can wait indefinitely for the raw response. This
path checks successful raw-frame receipt and does not deserialize
or validate that the response is SUPPORTED. Ordinary request traffic does not
reset the periodic schedule. A server DOWN event uses this probing mechanism
rather than blindly discarding live connections; event interpretation is specified
in [metadata and events](metadata-control-events.md).

items.text:
Session-wide switches enter a 32-element cluster request queue. The cluster
worker processes one fanout at a time, records the desired keyspace for future
nodes, and concurrently switches the nodes in one retained cluster snapshot.
It accepts the next switch only when the previous fanout finishes, while still
processing topology and connectivity updates. Racing calls have no prescribed
winner. Cancelling a caller after cluster enqueueing does not withdraw that
fanout while the cluster remains alive.

items.text:
The pool records the requested keyspace before switching a snapshot of its active
connections concurrently. If it has no active connections, the pool request
succeeds immediately and future connections inherit the keyspace. Otherwise it
tracks completions while continuing to process connection errors and refill
events. Only one keyspace switch is processed at a time; later switch requests
can wait in the one-element request queue. New connections can be prepared for
the new keyspace while the snapshot switch is in progress.

items.text:
Once a pool switch request has entered that queue, dropping the caller's waiting
future does not withdraw it or cancel an in-progress switch while the pool remains
alive. The worker still changes its desired keyspace, sends USE, and applies
failure handling; it ignores failure to deliver the final result to the departed
caller. The switch snapshot retains its own connection references. Removing those
connections from the active pool, including during resharding, does not remove
them from the pending switch or its result aggregation.

items.text:
A live connection that fails USE for a non-broken-connection reason is removed
from the active pool when the worker processes that result. Subsequent published
snapshots exclude it, but references retained from earlier snapshots are not
revoked and can still use its previous keyspace.
Already-broken connections are removed through normal failure monitoring. The
snapshot switch has one shared deadline, set to the connect timeout when the pool
starts processing it; waiting in the keyspace request queue is outside that
deadline. When the worker selects the expired-deadline branch, all
still-outstanding connections are removed and the switch reports timeout. Ready
completion events compete with that branch; there is no deadline-first priority
when both are ready. New connections that cannot establish the current
keyspace are never published. The requested keyspace remains current after
failure; this is not a rollback transaction.

items.text:
Across the completed snapshot, any error other than a broken-connection error
causes failure. At least one success plus only broken-connection failures counts
as success, because replacements will inherit the new keyspace. If all snapshot
requests fail with broken-connection errors, return such an error. This aggregation
does not guarantee that every node was reachable or every connection switched
successfully. Concurrent application requests can race with a switch; the pool
does not offer a global atomic keyspace-change barrier.

items.text:
The cluster uses the same aggregation rule for node results. A disabled node
returns success without sending USE, as does an enabled node whose pool has no
active connections. These no-op successes can satisfy the aggregation's success
condition, so an overall successful switch need not mean that any server has
validated the requested keyspace.

items.text:
Publish the updated connection snapshot before notifying initialization waiters
and emitting connectivity events. With a configured internal connectivity-event
sender, Initializing or Broken to Ready emits Established; Ready to Broken emits
Lost; the first Initializing to Broken also emits Lost. Ready-to-Ready and
Broken-to-Broken updates produce no connectivity transition event. Event send
failure is ignored.
Data-node pools always have this sender, independently of whether a public host
listener is configured. The cluster worker consumes the events and updates its
recorded status before optionally invoking that listener; its callback filtering
and timing are specified in the
[host listener contract](metadata-control-events.md#host-listener-event-contract).
Removing the last active connection additionally tries a nonblocking pool-empty
notification; a full notification channel already represents a pending signal.
This separate notification is sent before the updated snapshot is published, so
its receiver can wake while the published pool still appears Ready. Data-node
pools discard this separate receiver and use connectivity events.

items.text:
Rust-specific implementation choices include atomically published reference-counted
pool snapshots; a worker with concurrent sets of connection-opening, error, and
keyspace-switch futures; reader/writer/orphan/keepalive futures joined within one
router task; and a stream-handler map whose mutex is never held across a suspension
point. Connection monitors retain weak references, so monitoring alone does not
keep a removed connection alive. These are evidence of the observed behavior,
not requirements that a Go implementation reproduce the same data structures.

items.text:
The router receives a configuration clone before OPTIONS negotiation. Ordinary
response parsing uses the connection's subsequently negotiated protocol features
and effective compressor. Event parsing instead uses default protocol features
and the router's original compression configuration; these are not updated when
discovery completes or an unsupported requested compressor is cleared on the
connection. See [send_request and parse_response](https://github.com/scylladb/scylla-rust-driver/blob/f8b0ee928dc0dcb475247dc82cce4e42804b0621/scylla/src/network/connection.rs#L1459-L1525),
[router construction](https://github.com/scylladb/scylla-rust-driver/blob/f8b0ee928dc0dcb475247dc82cce4e42804b0621/scylla/src/network/connection.rs#L577-L618),
and [event parsing](https://github.com/scylladb/scylla-rust-driver/blob/f8b0ee928dc0dcb475247dc82cce4e42804b0621/scylla/src/network/connection.rs#L1939-L1983).

items.text:
The reference is not zero-copy throughout: requests are serialized to owned
buffers, ordinary pool snapshots clone connection references, gathering all
connections allocates a vector, and missing-shard fallback allocates a vector of
shards to randomize. A Go zero-copy/allocation contract must be specified and
measured independently rather than inferred from this implementation.

Concurrent session USE propagation is deliberately replaced by initial/qualified/v5 per-request keyspace. Rust unbounded queues, ignored cancellation races and identity-only diagnostics are not copied as defects.

For temporal tests use a controlled clock and explicitly distinguish exactly 1024
old orphans from 1025, and the age boundary from the periodic observation tick.
Schedule cancellation before queue submission, after queueing, after stream
assignment, concurrently with response dispatch, and after stream reuse. Force
an orphan notification to be consumed before allocation and check that the later
stream is absent from orphan-age tracking. Include
unsolicited streams, ignored negative streams, full event channels, shutdown with
queued requests, and failed keepalive while ordinary responses are arriving.

For keyspace tests interleave a switch, newly opened connections, refill failures,
another queued switch, application requests, caller cancellation after enqueueing,
retained connections removed by resharding, and simultaneously ready completion
and timeout branches. Assert the desired
keyspace after failure and which connections remain selectable rather than only
checking the returned error. Keepalive tests must distinguish OPTIONS receipt
from protocol-response validation; coalescing tests must distinguish preserved
results from throughput or latency claims. Do not infer a graceful drain,
identity-enforcement guarantee, or an all-stages connect timeout from defaults.

use the control connection and dedicated metadata timeouts, independently of

not change their consistency, timeout, retry, load-balancing, or speculation
behavior. Schema-agreement reads have a separate execution path described below.

items.text:
An explicit metadata refresh always requests a full fetch according to the
schema-fetch configuration. Its successful completion means the resulting
snapshot has been published, not merely that metadata queries have finished.
Already-started full fetches cannot satisfy a newly received explicit request:
the request remains queued until a subsequent full fetch can start. The driver
does not guarantee agreement among the system tables while reading them.
Cancelling a caller after its refresh request has been enqueued does not retract
the request or cancel its fetch; the eventual reply is simply ignored if that
caller is gone. Refresh completion is not a barrier for every server event already
received: events arriving during its full fetch can still require later work, and
coalescing can satisfy several callers through one later published snapshot.

All addresses returned for each contact-point hostname are considered, alongside
literal socket addresses, and duplicate socket addresses are removed. After any
non-timeout lookup error, the original hostname string is retried with port 9042;
this is not limited to strings lacking a port. Each lookup has its own timeout,
and failure of the fallback returns the original error. A timed-out first lookup
is not retried this way. Hostname resolutions run concurrently; individual failures
are logged and omitted. If no contact point resolves, session creation fails.
Contact points are direct addresses, not input to peer address translation.

items.text:
Candidates are tried sequentially in a shuffled known-peer order. Opening a
candidate includes event registration, then a full configured metadata fetch.
Server events are drained concurrently even during this first fetch: otherwise
an event burst could fill the connection's event queue and prevent the same
connection from reading metadata responses. Fetch-triggering events observed
during establishment of the retained candidate are carried forward as outstanding
work because the initial read may predate them. A rejected or failed candidate's
fetch plan is discarded; if no connection is retained, recovery performs another
full fetch. Status hints already sent by that candidate remain independently queued.

items.text:
After initial creation, a known-peer pass yielding neither a retained connection
nor usable metadata causes the original contact points to be resolved again and
retried. Usable metadata from rejected peers ends that pass successfully without
the contact-point fallback. The fallback uses the deduplicated socket-address
sort order, without another shuffle. On the initial attempt there is no second
resolution pass. Opening failures move to the next candidate. After a connection
opens, an initial metadata-fetch failure permits startup with dummy
metadata: known endpoints, generated host IDs, approximately evenly spaced
synthetic tokens, no location/schema/cluster-name information. Previously obtained
valid metadata from a rejected candidate is preferred to dummy metadata. That
candidate connection is discarded, and background recovery starts. If no
connection can be opened, session creation fails rather than using dummy data.

A successfully fetched topology replaces the future control-connection candidate
list, filtered through the host filter, before that topology can be published.
Valid metadata from a rejected peer is retained while other candidates are tried;
if all metadata-producing peers are rejected, metadata may be published without
retaining a control connection. Rejection of every discovered node is logged and
leaves the session unable to execute user queries through those nodes.

items.text:
There is an implementation limitation: the post-fetch rejection check recognizes
only a discovered-peer endpoint whose address matches the metadata. An initial
contact-point endpoint is not matched by that check, so it can remain the control
connection even if the host filter rejects the corresponding discovered peer.
Host filtering therefore is not a promise that bootstrap/control traffic never
touches rejected hosts.
The rejection check runs when selecting a candidate, not after ordinary full or
partial fetches on an established control connection. A later filter change or
topology result can disable that host's query pool and remove it from future
candidates without moving its existing control connection. That connection stays
until a failure or another control-replacement condition occurs.

items.text:
The full fetch reads peers, keyspaces, and (when configured) client routes
concurrently. Topology reads `system.peers` and the local row in `system.local`;
there is no `peers_v2` fallback in this implementation. Each node contains host ID,
broadcast RPC address, the control endpoint's port, optional datacenter/rack, and
tokens. Rows from both tables use the advertised RPC address as a translatable
peer address, including the local row. The connected socket IP is not substituted
for a bad advertised address. The optional cluster name comes from the local row.
Only full fetches replace the stored cluster name; partial topology fetches
discard that field. The public cluster-name accessor returns an empty string
when no name is known, including during dummy-metadata startup.

items.text:
Invalid topology rows/query-stream errors are logged and skipped, as are rows
with null host IDs. A null token list means zero tokens. If any token text cannot
be parsed as a signed 64-bit token, that node gets a random dummy token instead
of failing the whole fetch. The aggregate peer list is rejected if it is empty or
every peer has an empty token list. Individual zero-token nodes are retained and
exposed in the public node list even though absent from the token ring.
This tolerance includes a failure to prepare or start either topology query and
a failure partway through paging. If the surviving rows satisfy the aggregate
checks, that incomplete peer list is accepted as a replacement; nodes omitted by
the failed read can disappear from the snapshot. Such a read does not itself
schedule a retry or replacement control connection.

items.text:
Topology validation does not reject duplicate host IDs, socket addresses, or
tokens. When several accepted rows have the same host ID, the public node map
keeps the last processed row's node, while the ring retains tokens and node
references from every row. Conflicting rows can therefore leave ring entries
referring to a different node object/address than lookup by that host ID returns.
The concurrently read peer/local streams do not give such duplicates a stable
winner. Atomic publication does not validate this inconsistent server input.

items.text:
UDTs are dependency-sorted before construction, including references nested in
collections/tuples/vectors. Cycles and syntactically invalid UDT field types are
fetch errors. Missing UDT definitions are a recoverable error at keyspace scope.
Partition/clustering key positions must be contiguous from zero after sorting;
gaps, negative positions, or duplicate positions invalidate a listed table/view
and therefore that keyspace's fetched schema. This does not require a nonempty
partition key: a table/view listed without matching column rows is retained with
empty columns/keys and no partitioner, even at full detail. Column kinds are
partition key, clustering, regular, or static.
For rows that reach their respective validation steps, malformed column type
syntax or unknown kinds fail the fetch. Columns whose type string is exactly
`empty` are omitted before type/kind validation, regardless of their name.
A prior missing-UDT error for the keyspace skips column type/kind parsing and
propagates that recoverable error; a column's own unresolved UDT likewise skips
its kind validation. Recoverable table errors only reach the keyspace if that
table/view is returned by the subsequent name query. Leftover column definitions
and their recoverable errors are discarded when no table/view name matches;
the parser does not require all schema tables to describe the same objects.
Collection frozen state, tuple members, vector
dimensions, and UDT field order are represented. Vector dimensions parse as unsigned
16-bit decimal values, including zero; this metadata parser does not enforce a
positive dimension. UDT field names and parsed field types are zipped, so a length
mismatch truncates to the shorter list rather than producing a length error.

`system_schema.scylla_tables` supplies partitioners. Missing-table/column
compatibility falls back to no per-table override. `system_schema.scylla_keyspaces`
supplies tablet status when `initial_tablets` is non-null. With tablet-routing-v2
negotiated, the driver first also reads `consistency`; if unsupported it retries
without that column. If the table is unsupported, all keyspaces default to
non-tablet/eventual. Only the exact `global` value denotes strong consistency;
unknown, absent, and other values mean eventual. The strong-consistency public
field and its enum require both `scylla_unstable` and
`unstable-strong-consistency`, although internal metadata still records it. Compatibility
detection treats any database `Invalid` error in the relevant request-error shape
as a missing table/column, not only errors proven to have that cause.

items.text:
Recoverable errors in a single keyspace preserve that keyspace's previous valid
schema. Without an older version, the keyspace is omitted until a later successful
fetch. Other keyspaces can still update. The failed keyspace is scheduled again
at a later schema tick; a newer event (particularly a drop) takes precedence over
that retry. Errors outside this recoverable category fail the containing fetch.
An explicit refresh can therefore succeed while retaining stale keyspace metadata
or omitting a newly discovered malformed keyspace; it does not wait for those
keyspaces' retries. In a partial batch containing both drops and rereads, a
nonrecoverable reread error also prevents publication of that batch's drops;
the entire failed batch is superseded by the scheduled full fetch.
A requested keyspace whose reread returns no keyspace row is removed, even if no
keyspace-drop event was received; absence is distinct from a recoverable error.

exists, while connected means the pool currently reports at least one connection.
An enabled node can be disconnected, and a disabled node reports disconnected.

token/endpoint inspection, including optional preserialized interop helpers, is
specified in [routing](routing.md#partition-keys-tokens-and-vnode-placement).
Session keyspace switching shares the cluster worker but follows the separate
[connection propagation contract](connections.md#keyspace-propagation-and-failure).

items.text:
Status notifications are hints, never authoritative liveness assignments. UP
wakes the pool worker and requests a refill-backoff reset. A needed refill still
uses the refill policy's delay and waits for an already-running refill to finish;
it does not guarantee immediate connection opening. The pool scheduling details
are in [connections](connections.md#filling-excess-connections-and-backoff).
DOWN requests an immediate keepalive probe on current connections; a successful
probe leaves them usable. The hints match known nodes by untranslated broadcast socket address,
not by translated connection endpoint. Unknown addresses are harmless no-ops.
Within unapplied updates, only the latest UP/DOWN hint per address survives.

items.text:
Only one fetch of each partial type may run at a time. Topology, schema, and
client-route partial fetches may run concurrently with one another. Repeated
topology requests collapse to one outstanding reread; client-route pairs are
deduplicated; only the latest schema change per keyspace is retained. Schema work
waits for the periodic tick, even when it is the only work pending. Ticks advance
without work, avoiding immediate synchronized schema reads across clients. A
schema event arriving while a schema read is running can require another later
tick; this is batching, not a debounce timer restarted on every event.

items.text:
A due full fetch cancels running partial fetches and subsumes previously recorded
partial work. Events received after that full fetch starts remain owed and are
processed after it completes. Full fetches exclude other fetches in the metadata
worker's scheduler. This cancellation drops partial-fetch futures and prevents
their results from being published; it does not guarantee that their network
requests have stopped. Later pages run in spawned pager tasks that hold the
connection and discover a dropped consumer when sending a page or error, so their
page requests can overlap the full fetch. Already submitted requests are not
cancelled at the server.
Starting a full fetch resets the periodic deadline. The deadline timer is disabled
while a full fetch runs. If another event wakes the loop after the deadline, the
deadline advances even though that full fetch prevents new work; that tick is not
saved for later. Otherwise an overdue deadline can start work after completion.
Deadlines advance from the time they are processed, with no replay of missed ticks.
A duration too large to add to the clock falls back to an immediately due deadline.
With the normal periodic mode and no affected keyspaces, a tick performs no metadata
query; missed events are therefore not repaired by routine ticks. Full mode is the
escape hatch.

items.text:
The event-draining loop does not directly await metadata fetches or state
publication: it multiplexes events, fetch outcomes, refresh requests, and timers.
Failure of a partial fetch schedules a full fetch. Failure of a full fetch marks
the control connection unusable and enters replacement. Broken connections do
the same and abandon outstanding partial work because replacement fetches all
configured metadata. Repair starts immediately, then no more often than once
per second measured from the previous attempt's start (a slower attempt need not
sleep again). An explicit refresh received during repair wait triggers an early
attempt. A pending explicit refresh survives replacement; a failed replacement
attempt reports its error to that requester, while background repair continues.

items.text:
The metadata worker hands updates to the cluster-state worker through one pending
mergeable slot. This bounds queued update objects, not the number of keyspaces,
route pairs, hints, or waiting refresh responses within the object. It avoids
blocking server-event draining while the state worker rebuilds its snapshot.
The newest full metadata replaces older pending full/partial data, preserving
all explicit refresh response handles. Later partial results modify only their
own aspect. A newer broken keyspace result does not overwrite an older valid
pending keyspace. A drop removes it. Different partial aspects merge independently;
the newest topology replaces the whole pending peer list.

items.text:
Pending absence is not a durable tombstone: a later recoverable error can replace
an unapplied keyspace drop, either in partial merging or in a newer full fetch.
When that error is applied, fallback consults the last published snapshot and can
reuse the pre-drop schema. If the drop was already published, there is no older
keyspace to reuse. Thus drop/recreate/error outcomes can depend on whether the
state worker consumed the drop before the newer result arrived.

items.text:
Published topology/schema/replica information is an atomically replaced immutable
snapshot. Readers may retain an older snapshot safely. Node objects themselves
reference mutable connection pools, so a retained snapshot is not a frozen view
of connectivity. Partial updates share topology or the schema map when that
aspect is untouched, and retain unaffected keyspace/node objects and pools.
Full refreshes always construct a new topology container, schema map, locator,
and snapshot, even if their values are unchanged; reusable nodes/pools and
keyspaces retained after recoverable errors can still be shared. An unchanged
partial topology update and already-resolved duplicate tablet feedback publish
no new snapshot; repeated feedback with unresolved replicas still rebuilds state.
A schema partial update still constructs a schema map/snapshot; the implementation
does not suppress it merely because values compare equal.

items.text:
Node identity is keyed by host ID. Unchanged enabled state, address, datacenter,
and rack permit object reuse. For an enabled node whose address alone changes,
the node object is replaced while its pool is retained and notified of the new
address. Datacenter/rack or enabled-state changes can require a new pool/object.
Filtered nodes remain represented without pools and may remain in ring metadata.
The public node list includes all known nodes, including disabled and zero-token
nodes. Host-filter changes are evaluated when topology is processed.
Public `Node::is_scylladb()` is an optional connection-derived observation based
on negotiated extensions; it can be unknown without an available pool. Its
sampling and sharding-independent detection are detailed in
[connection establishment](connections.md#connection-establishment-and-negotiated-properties).
Retained snapshots or node handles also retain their pools, even after removal or
replacement in the current topology. An address-only change updates the shared
pool's endpoint during construction of the new state, before publication; an old
node can therefore still report its old address while sharing a pool already
targeting the new endpoint. Removing a node from the current snapshot does not
itself close every pool retained by older readers.

items.text:
Host callbacks run synchronously during initial session construction and,
afterward, on the cluster worker; they can delay construction or subsequent state
work. There is no asynchronous public event queue or durable event history.
Events include host ID and broadcast socket address. Addition reporting requires
the new node to be enabled; removal reporting requires the old node to be enabled.
Address-change candidates require only the old node to be enabled, so an address
change can still be reported when the new address causes the node to be filtered.
Removal and address-change reporting additionally require a recorded listener
status for that host ID; a missing status is logged and the notifications are
skipped.

items.text:
Removed nodes are processed before address changes, then additions; iteration
order among nodes within each group is unspecified. A change only in the internal
address-translation marker does not emit `AddressChanged`. Topology membership
differences are keyed by ID: merely enabling/disabling an existing ID through a
changing filter does not inherently produce `Added`/`Removed` notifications.
In particular, a host first discovered while disabled has no recorded listener
status. Enabling that same known ID later does not create one, so its subsequent
pool-connectivity events are ignored even though its query pool can work.
Later address changes and removal of that enabled host also produce no listener
notifications while that status remains absent. Removal from the topology still
takes effect; a later enabled reappearance after removal is a new addition and
can establish listener status.
Connectivity events carry only a host ID, without a pool identity, generation,
or event-time address. They are interpreted against the current snapshot and
recorded status when consumed. A queued event, or an event from an old pool kept
alive by a retained snapshot, can therefore affect notifications for a replacement
node with the same ID and use that node's current address. There is no check that
the emitting pool is the current node's pool, that the current node is enabled,
or that its state still matches the event at delivery time.

items.text:
Client routes are queried only when configured. Full route reads are filtered by
the subscriber's connection IDs. At the internal subscriber/query boundary, an
empty full-read filter means unrestricted; public client-routes configuration
requires a nonempty proxy/connection-ID list, so it cannot select that case.
Partial event handling filters affected pairs by literal membership in the
subscriber list, so an empty subscriber list selects no event pairs. The query
uses connection-ID and host-ID sets and can return their cross product; only
the originally requested relevant pairs are applied. A requested pair missing
from the result deletes that route. Deleting a host's final route removes its
empty route map. Newer updates win per pair and preserve disjoint pairs.
Changed routes can trigger refills using the newly installed route information;
route selection and connection replacement details are specified elsewhere.

items.text:
Route reads fail as a whole on query, row-decoding, or port-conversion errors;
there is no missing-table compatibility fallback for `system.client_routes`.
Non-null ports must fit an unsigned 16-bit integer, including zero; the metadata
parser permits both ports to be null. Every returned row is decoded and validated
before filtering the cross product, so even a malformed unrequested pair can fail
the partial fetch. A failed route partial escalates to a full fetch, and a failed
route read within a full fetch fails that full fetch; valid topology/schema data
from the same full fetch is not published separately.

items.text:
Tablet feedback travels separately from control events in a bounded channel of
8192 entries and is drained in batches of up to that size. The state worker
compares each feedback item against the state already updated by earlier items
in the batch. A batch avoids cloning/publication only when every item exactly
matches its stored range, version, ordered replicas, and shards, with all replicas
resolved. A stored tablet with unresolved replicas never counts as a duplicate,
so even identical repeated payloads can rebuild and publish state. New tablet
information may be stored even if its keyspace is not yet known. Unknown replica
host IDs are initially omitted from resolved replicas. Maintenance retries their
resolution and discards a tablet if any replica remains unknown; tablets referring
to removed nodes are also discarded. Topology/schema updates maintain tablet
entries for tablet-based tables and views, remove obsolete information, and replace
references to recreated nodes.
The replica/range/version conflict rules are owned by the routing specification.

items.text:
An agreement check queries each node with working connections concurrently,
reading its local schema version at consistency ONE with an idempotent internal
statement. These are unprepared, unpaged QUERYs sent through ordinary node pools,
including zero-token nodes when their pools have working connections. They bypass
the control connection, metadata SELECT timeouts, and session execution-profile
load balancing, retry, speculation, and request-timeout settings. Connections
within one node are tried in sequence until one succeeds.
If all its connections fail, a non-broken-connection error takes priority over
broken-connection errors. Nodes with only broken connections may be ignored if
some other node provides a schema version. No usable node/only broken connections
is an error, not vacuous agreement. Equal versions from successful nodes establish
agreement; different versions mean agreement has not yet been reached.
The one-shot API returns the agreed schema-version UUID when there is agreement,
absence when versions differ, or an error; the waiting API returns the agreed
UUID or an error.

items.text:
Each check retains one topology snapshot and takes working-connection handles
from its pools; it does not incorporate nodes added to a newer snapshot while
that check runs. All per-node reads are awaited before results are evaluated,
including when one has already failed. Each retry takes a fresh snapshot.
The one-shot check has no agreement timeout wrapper; the configured agreement
deadline bounds the waiting API, including its in-progress check. Agreement
does not freeze schema changes after the versions have been read.

items.text:
Automatic agreement after a schema-changing result additionally requires the
statement coordinator to provide a successful version. Its absence or broken
connections cannot be silently ignored. This guards against observing agreement
among other nodes that have not yet learned the coordinator's schema change.
The optional interop waiting API can also require a caller-specified host ID,
using the same checks, retries, and deadline; omitting that ID behaves like the
ordinary manual wait. It requires both `scylla_unstable` and
`unstable-csharp-rs`. Like other manual agreement calls, this API does not refresh
metadata after agreement.

items.text:
Waiting checks immediately, then sleeps the configured interval after an
unsuccessful/transient result, under the overall agreement deadline. Connection
pool errors, missing required hosts, broken connections, stream exhaustion,
several response parse errors, overload/timeouts, unprepared, rate limiting, and
bootstrapping are retryable here. Serialization/unexpected response failures,
malformed row results, authorization/configuration/syntax/protocol failures,
unavailable/read-or-write-failure/server/unknown database errors, and inconsistent
prepared IDs stop waiting. If the deadline expires and the last completed check
failed, that check's error is returned. If no check completed, or the last completed
check succeeded but found differing versions, a timeout is returned; a later
version mismatch therefore supersedes an earlier error. Consequently this API
does not always return a timeout error when the wait deadline was exhausted.
