items.text:
With automatic waiting enabled, a schema-changing statement can succeed on the
server yet return an automatic-agreement/metadata-refresh error to its caller.
Successful automatic agreement then performs a full metadata refresh by default.
Both steps follow successful core request execution and run outside that
statement's request deadline; the agreement deadline bounds only the waiting
step, not the subsequent refresh. Disabling automatic waiting also bypasses this
refresh even if its separate flag remains enabled. The same handling applies to
an automatic pager's first schema-change response, as described in
[execution](execution.md#results-timestamps-and-response-side-effects).
Manual agreement calls do not themselves refresh metadata.

items.text:
Dropping the cluster's worker handles/channels ends background work. The merge
channel delivers a last pending value before reporting that its sender is gone;
cancelled receives do not lose updates. Sending after receiver drop is rejected.
This does not synchronously tear down pools retained through external snapshots
or node handles, or abort already spawned pager and blocking locator tasks.
Unexpected loss of the control connection's failure sender is treated as runtime
shutdown. The source explicitly records a known issue: if an explicit refresh is
pending when this happens, the dropped reply channel can make the refresh caller
panic. This is recorded source behavior, not a desirable Go API contract.

items.text:
Metadata SELECTs are prepared and cached by original query text across control
connection replacements, marked idempotent, and paged at 1024 rows. Each execution
uses a prepared-statement clone with the current client timeout. The fixed-connection
pager applies that timeout afresh to the first page and every later page; the initial
cache-miss PREPARE happens before that timeout is installed. There is no overall
metadata-fetch deadline here. Metadata pages use a fixed connection with a
fallthrough retry policy: normal session retries, failover, and speculation do not
apply to an individual page. The connection layer can still reprepare and resend
EXECUTE once after `UNPREPARED`, within that page's deadline. Other failures follow
the topology tolerance, compatibility fallback, or worker recovery rules above.
The server-side timeout is encoded in whole milliseconds
in the prepared query when prepared, truncating submillisecond precision. Cache
hits do not render that query again or reevaluate the current server family:
the cached statement retains whether its original preparation included
`USING TIMEOUT`. Consequently, switching the control connection between server
families does not add or remove that clause; `UNPREPARED` recovery also reprepares
the cached query text on the new server. Explicit
refresh and keyspace request queues each have capacity 32. Pool-connectivity events use an
unbounded channel. Snapshot publication uses `ArcSwap`; retained `Arc<Node>` pool
handles explain the mutable-connectivity qualification above. Locator rebuilding
is offloaded with `spawn_blocking`. These are implementation mechanisms, not
requirements to copy Rust primitives into Go.

The inspection API exposes borrowed keyspaces, an iterator of borrowed names and
keyspaces, a slice of shared node handles, and optional lookup by host ID.
Rust `Node` equality and hashing use only host ID, even when distinct retained
node objects have different addresses or pools. `ColumnKind::from_str` accepts

The schema-event test injects a final keyspace-drop event to assert a query-free
removal. Its real-server drop-query-count assertion is commented out because a
server can emit a table-drop event after the keyspace-drop event. The last event
then wins and causes a reread; this catalog does not claim query-free removal for
every real DDL event ordering.

items.text:
Use controlled clocks for tick boundaries, refresh arrival during a full fetch,
repair attempts longer than one second, and schema events during pending schema
work. Cover events arriving after the periodic deadline during a long full fetch,
overflowing refresh durations, and separate deadlines for successive metadata pages.
Inject more than 32 control events while metadata responses are withheld.
Test dropped/recreated keyspaces and recoverable errors before and after merging;
retain old snapshots while changing host addresses and filter outcomes. Include
zero-token nodes, null/malformed peer data, unsupported Scylla schema tables,
multiple DNS addresses with duplicates, no resolvable/reachable peers, and route
cross-product rows. Exercise the default-port DNS fallback after non-timeout errors,
including its original-error preservation, and malformed schema with no column rows,
unequal UDT field lists, and zero/overflowing vector dimensions.
Separate a failed topology query with surviving valid peers from a wholly unusable
peer list. Inject malformed route rows outside the requested pairs, a failed
reread batched with a keyspace drop, and `UNPREPARED` during a metadata page; assert
the exact publication/recovery boundary and the unchanged per-page deadline.
Agreement tests must distinguish mismatch, required-host
absence, mixed broken/successful nodes, nontransient errors, and the last completed
check's outcome at deadline, including an error followed by a version mismatch.
Listener tests must assert per-host ordering without imposing an order on
independent hosts or assuming callbacks run after publication. Retain a replaced
node's old pool, then deliver its connectivity event after publication; distinguish
its host ID from the current pool's identity. Cancel a refresh after enqueue and
preempt a partial fetch with an outstanding later page, checking separately that
the discarded result cannot publish and that network work may continue. Coalesce
a keyspace drop with a later recoverable error and compare with publishing the
drop first. Change topology while schema agreement is reading its captured nodes,
and verify that only a subsequent check uses the new membership.
Exercise the optional required-host waiting API with both an absent ID and no
required ID. Keep a control connection open while its host becomes filtered,
and verify separately the query-pool and control-candidate changes. Reuse a
metadata statement cache across control connections with different negotiated
server families and check the retained timeout clause, including reprepare.
Enable a host that was initially filtered out and inspect both its working pool
and the absence of listener status/notifications; then change its address, remove
it, and readd it enabled to check when listener reporting resumes. Compare equal full refreshes
with unchanged partial topology updates to distinguish publication/container
replacement from node/pool reuse.
Remap the session's default profile and capture metadata EXECUTE consistency and
timeouts separately from schema-version QUERYs on node pools. Include a working
zero-token node in agreement checks. Delay automatic agreement past the original
statement deadline, then delay its subsequent refresh past the agreement deadline;
also disable automatic waiting while leaving refresh enabled.
Repeat identical tablet feedback with an unknown replica and distinguish its
new snapshot from the no-publication case after all replicas resolve.
Return conflicting peer/local rows with the same host ID and inspect both the
public node map and every ring entry; include repeated addresses and tokens.
Combine a missing UDT with malformed column types or unknown kinds to check
validation precedence. Omit a table/view name while retaining its column rows,
distinguishing a discarded recoverable key error from a fetch-wide syntax error.

Manual paging begins with a start state and accepts a returned continuation on
the next single-page call. Continuation bytes can be exported, retained, and
restored; the driver neither interprets them nor binds them to a query, values,
or session. Restoring bytes does not validate that they belong to the requested
query. A start state has no bytes; an explicitly supplied empty byte sequence is
still a continuation, and a response containing it still means more pages.
Completion is a separate response state, not a reusable start token. Each manual
page call resolves its own profile and cluster snapshot and can use a different
coordinator; it does not inherit the automatic pager's coordinator preference.

section: Statements, execution, paging, retry, and speculation
items.text:
A profile is immutable after construction. A handle can be redirected to a new
profile, and every clone of that handle observes the redirection for later
requests. Separately created handles can point to the same profile and later be
remapped independently. An already running request retains its resolved profile.
An automatic pager resolves configuration once at creation; remapping the handle
does not reconfigure its later pages. Cloning a statement copies its configuration
and preserves shared handles and policy objects rather than creating independent
policy instances. The snapshot selects policy objects; it does not freeze their
internal state, such as load-balancing feedback or metrics used by speculation.
In Rust, resolution occurs when the asynchronous body reaches the handle load,
not when an unpolled future is constructed. Preparation and serialization that
precede that load can therefore finish after a handle has been remapped.

Regular and serial overrides can be unset to restore profile inheritance.
Clearing an individual retry/load-balancing policy restores the selected profile's
policy; clearing the profile handle restores the session's default handle.
Statement option getters expose stored overrides, not resolved effective settings.
In particular, the serial-consistency getter returns no value both for inheritance
and for explicit omission, even though those states execute differently. The
cached-metadata getter likewise reports the configured preference, not the
negotiated connection behavior. Profiles and handles can produce builders
initialized from their current settings; a profile obtained from a handle is a
snapshot and does not follow subsequent handle remapping. Optional handle labels
serve debugging only.

items.text:
For unpaged or single-page execution of an unprepared query with no bound values,
each attempt sends the query string directly. With nonempty bound values, each
attempt first prepares the query on the chosen connection, validates and serializes
the values against that metadata, and executes it on that connection. This local
preparation is part of the attempt and therefore within the request deadline.
The coordinator was already chosen without a partition token, table, or confirmed
conditional-write flag. Local preparation does not restart routing with the newly
learned token. Token calculation for a tablet hint is best effort on this path:
failure omits useful hint information rather than failing the query.
This connection-local preparation retains the default Murmur3 partitioner;
unlike explicit session preparation, it does not install the table's partitioner
from cluster metadata before calculating that hint.

items.text:
Preparation takes a cluster snapshot and first sends a prepare request concurrently
on one selected working connection per node. It waits for every attempted
preparation to finish. One successful response suffices even when other nodes
failed, provided the successful prepared identifiers agree. If that preparation
pass returns an error, a fallback pass attempts preparation across working shard
connections. The second pass also waits for all attempts. No working connection
or failure of all contacted connections produces a preparation error. Failure to
obtain the initial working-connection iterator returns immediately, before the
fallback pass.

items.text:
Ordinary prepared execution serializes supplied values before entering the core
request deadline. It calculates the partition key/token when available and uses
the table, token, and confirmed conditional-write flag for routing. Failure to
find an indexed serialized value or calculate a token is an execution error on
this path, unlike the best-effort hint calculation for unprepared queries.
NULL and UNSET partition-key entries are present values and are skipped by token
extraction, rather than producing a missing-index error. The driver can therefore
hash only the remaining components or empty input; token calculation does not
establish that the partition key is legal. See [routing](routing.md) for the
component-encoding rules.
The same serialized values are reused across attempts. An automatic prepared
pager retains its serialized values for every page.

items.text:
When execution receives an unprepared-statement response, the connection
prepares the original query again on that same connection and resends execution
once. The newly prepared ID must equal the original ID; otherwise execution
fails with both identities and statement context. An unprepared response to the
resend is returned to the outer execution machinery. This repair is inside one
attempt and is independent of the user's retry policy and idempotence flag.
For a single EXECUTE, the ID named by the unprepared error is logged but is not
compared with the executed ID: even an unrelated reported ID triggers repair of
the original statement. The identity check applies to the subsequent PREPARED
response. Batch repair instead uses the error's ID to locate a member.

items.text:
Tablet feedback is processed only for EXECUTE responses, including this resend.
Native QUERY and BATCH responses do not update the tablet cache. An unprepared
query with values can update it because that path sends EXECUTE after preparation.
When prepared table identity is available, feedback is forwarded before the
response's database error is interpreted, so failed EXECUTEs, including the
initial unprepared response, can also update routing. Valid feedback uses an
awaited send to the cluster worker's bounded queue. A full queue can delay the
attempt or let its deadline expire after the server has already replied; a closed
receiver is ignored. Enqueueing does not wait for publication of a new cluster
snapshot. Already enqueued feedback can be applied after cancellation, while a
pending send can be dropped. These boundaries are detailed in
[routing](routing.md#tablet-placement-and-feedback).

Without negotiated metadata-ID support, suppressing response metadata is opt-in.
That opt-in does not validate cached metadata against schema changes; stale
metadata can cause decoding errors or silently misinterpreted values. Transparent
reprepare without a metadata ID does not refresh that result-metadata cache.

the statement's cache setting is false. Empty cached metadata forces a metadata
request; statements can return no metadata during preparation but rows during
execution. On extension-capable connections an empty metadata ID is sent when
there is no usable cached ID, including prepared objects obtained from an older
server in a mixed-version cluster. Connections without the extension never send
the extension's ID field.

items.text:
An EXECUTE row response carrying a different metadata ID updates the current
cache. The same ID also updates the cache if the cache was empty and the response
has columns. Reprepare updates the cache only when the server supplies an ID
different from the loaded cache snapshot; it skips an empty replacement when
that snapshot is nonempty. Skipping this cache update does not fail reprepare.
The same-ID/empty-cache exception above applies to row responses, not reprepare.
These checks and the replacement are separate operations, not an atomic
compare-and-swap. A concurrent execution can install nonempty metadata after
reprepare checks an empty snapshot, then have it overwritten by reprepare's empty
replacement. Concurrent responses install snapshots in store order, which need
not be response-arrival or schema-version order. Even a response decoded with an
older cached snapshot can reinstall that snapshot after another execution has
updated the cache. Already retained results and guards keep their own snapshots.

idempotence, timeout, and policies for the request.

Routing uses only the first member's table and token, and only if that member is
already prepared when the session builds the routing information. A later
prepared member does not supply a replacement routing key. First-member values
serialized for token extraction are cached and reused in batch serialization.
Other member values are serialized when the batch frame is sent, and can be
serialized again on outer retries and internal batch-repair resends. There is no
whole-batch snapshot of serialized values comparable to a bound statement.
If any already prepared member is a confirmed conditional write, the entire
batch is marked conditional for routing. Query strings are not parsed to infer
this flag. See [routing](routing.md) for the effect on target ordering.

items.text:
Before sending a batch, the chosen connection prepares unprepared query strings
whose value lists are nonempty. Repeated identical query text in that preparation
set is prepared once for the connection attempt. Queries requiring no values
remain unprepared unless they share text with a member selected for preparation.
This implicit preparation does not retroactively improve session-level batch
routing. Explicit batch preparation instead returns a new batch with all query
members prepared, preserves batch settings, leaves already prepared members
prepared, and prepares the remaining members concurrently. It does not deduplicate
equal query strings. A preparation failure returns no batch and drops member
futures still pending when the combined operation returns, although preparations
already sent can have server-side effects. There is no driver-level guarantee
that the first completed member error ends the combined operation immediately.
This differs from waiting for every connection attempt within each individual
statement's preparation pass. Connection-local implicit preparation
instead prepares the deduplicated query strings sequentially, in unspecified
set-iteration order, and stops on the first preparation error.

items.text:
The optional caching session wraps an existing session, optionally through shared
ownership. Its query APIs obtain a cached prepared statement and then call the
corresponding prepared API; batch execution prepares and caches unprepared
members as needed. An already fully prepared batch bypasses cache preparation.
The default builder capacity is 128; zero capacity is rejected as a programmer
error. A custom key hasher and result-metadata-cache preference can be supplied.
The metadata-cache preference defaults to false in all constructors and the
builder; negotiated metadata-ID support still determines effective caching.

items.text:
Cache keys are query strings only. They do not include current keyspace,
consistency, page size, values, or other statement options. Reusing unqualified
query text after a keyspace switch can therefore reuse a previously prepared
object; callers must not assume keyspace-scoped keys or invalidation. Each cache
lookup reconstructs a configured handle from the current call's statement
options and page size. Options from the first use do not leak into later uses.
The wrapper's metadata-cache preference is then applied to that handle.

items.text:
A miss prepares first, then evicts entries while the observed size is at least
the configured capacity, then inserts the prepared object. Eviction removes the
first entry returned by the concurrent map iterator: it is neither an LRU nor a
FIFO guarantee. Concurrent misses for the same query are not coalesced and can
prepare redundantly. The check/evict/insert sequence is not atomic, so capacity is
not a strict instantaneous bound under concurrency. The repeated eviction check
allows later insertions to repair excess size and can evict more than necessary.

prepared handles already returned or used by requests and pagers. Concurrent
misses for the same text each return their own prepared object, while the last
insertion determines what later cache hits use. Those independently prepared
objects have separate mutable result-metadata caches. Capacity limits map entries,
not all prepared state retained by callers or in-flight operations.

items.text:
A failed cache-miss preparation neither inserts a negative cache entry nor evicts
an existing entry for that miss. Cached batch preparation runs member lookups
concurrently and drops unfinished member futures when the combined operation
returns a member failure. It shares explicit batch preparation's error-delivery
timing limitation.
Successful members may already have inserted entries and evicted older ones;
those cache changes are not rolled back. Cache-miss preparation, including batch
members, precedes the underlying execution deadline and uses the explicit
preparation algorithm described above.

Request, attempt, deadline, and error boundaries
items.text:
A request resolves one cluster snapshot and constructs a load-balancing plan of
node/shard targets. Each attempt acquires a connection for its current target.
Failure to obtain a connection skips to the next target and retains the pool
error as the branch's last error. It does not invoke attempt
history callbacks, load-balancing failure feedback, or the retry policy, and does
not count as a sent or failed query attempt in query metrics. Once a connection
is acquired, the attempt count and history begin before serialization or local
preparation; an attempt can therefore fail without sending the final query,
execute, or batch frame. The retry policy is consulted after such an attempt
fails.

items.text:
A successful attempt returns its response and coordinator. An attempt error
notifies the load-balancing policy, then is supplied to the retry session with
the statement's idempotence and the **current** regular consistency. The history
listener receives the error together with the resulting retry decision. That
decision can stop, retry the same target, advance to the next target, or report an
ignored write error as success. Same-target retry picks
a connection again; it does not promise reuse of the same socket. A retry can
change regular consistency, and subsequent attempts and retry decisions see
that changed value. The plan's routing information retains the original routing
consistency; a downgrade does not rebuild routing information.

items.text:
Retry-session state is independent for every speculative branch and created
lazily on that branch's first failed attempt. A request with no targets returns
an empty-plan error. Exhaustion after attempts returns the last encountered
attempt/pool error. There is no driver-wide numeric retry limit: the plan,
selected retry policy, and deadline determine termination. A custom same-target
policy and disabled deadline can therefore retry indefinitely.

items.text:
The client timeout encloses connection picking, attempts, local prepare/execute
repair, retry loops, and speculative branches for that request. It is not a
server execution cancellation guarantee. It does not enclose prior ordinary
prepared-value serialization, first-member batch serialization, or partition-key/
token calculation done before the runner. Explicit session preparation and
post-success keyspace/schema side effects are also outside this deadline.
A timeout returns a distinct request-timeout error
and increments the timeout counter. Connection cleanup for a request abandoned
while the server is still executing belongs to [connections](connections.md).

attempt futures; it does not send a server-side cancellation or undo already
completed work. Dropping an execution future is distinct from the driver's
timeout path: it does not itself increment the timeout counter or finish the
request's history record. Attempts abandoned by caller cancellation, a timeout,
or a winning speculative branch can likewise retain a start event without a
success/error callback. Automatic paging after page one has the separate worker
lifetime described below.

Ignored-write success becomes an empty non-row result with its coordinator and
without warnings or a trace ID. For automatic paging it instead ends the stream;
if it happens on page one, the returned pager is empty. This result is explicitly
permitted by a selected retry policy; it is not proof the requested consistency
was satisfied. Its underlying failed attempt still increments the failure count,
reports load-balancing failure, and records the error and ignore decision in
attempt history. The logical request is then recorded as successful; no successful
attempt callback or latency sample is added for that ignored error.

The downgrading policy is an explicit opt-in and can weaken the requested
consistency or ignore a write timeout. It shares a single one-use budget across
unavailable/read-timeout/write-timeout handling. For a reported live/reply count,
its fallback is THREE for at least three, TWO for two, ONE for one; an original
EACH_QUORUM also permits ONE when the count is zero or negative. Otherwise it
stops. Error counts are decoded as signed integers without a nonnegative check.
The fallback is not clamped to the request's consistency: for example, an
unavailable response reporting two live replicas makes a request at ONE retry at
TWO. Despite its name, the policy does not guarantee that every changed
consistency is weaker than the previous one.

items.text:
Only statements explicitly marked idempotent use a configured speculative policy.
The policy supplies a maximum number of additional branches, excluding the
original branch, and an interval. The simple policy uses a fixed interval. The
metrics-dependent percentile policy obtains an interval in milliseconds from
recorded latency and falls back to 100 ms when that lookup fails. The percentile
policy and the metrics field of its context exist only with the `metrics` feature,
which is disabled by default. Fixed-interval and custom speculative policies
remain available without metrics.
The branch limit and interval are read once per logical request (once per page
for automatic paging). Later launches reuse that interval. An ignorable failure
does not launch a replacement immediately; it waits for the existing timer.

items.text:
Branches share a synchronized target-plan iterator, so each branch consumes new
plan entries rather than independently starting at the first target. Each branch
has independent retries and starts at the original effective consistency. A
successful branch or a terminal error ends the race immediately and drops the
other branch futures. A branch reporting a transient error can be ignored while
other branches run or while scheduled additional branches remain. When a branch
finds no remaining target at its start, the scheduler stops launching new branches
but waits for already running ones. A branch that used targets and then exhausted
the plan reports its last error instead; a later scheduled branch may still run
to observe the empty plan.
When all branches finish without a decisive result, the last ignorable error is
returned, or an empty-plan error when there was none.

Every retry or speculative branch for one page uses that page's same input
continuation. The continuation advances only after a successful row response.
Recovery does not replay earlier successful pages or retract rows already yielded
to the caller. A page failure ends background fetching; after receiving that
error, polling again cannot restart the failed fetch. The automatic pager exposes no
continuation token for manual resumption.
Continuation bytes are not checked for repetition or forward progress. Repeated
tokens can therefore refetch rows, and an endless sequence of successful empty
pages with continuations can keep a row poll pending indefinitely. There is no
total page-count or whole-stream deadline; completing each page within its own
deadline does not bound the duration of iteration.

section: Statements, execution, paging, retry, and speculation
items.text:
Page one is fetched on the caller's task. Only if it has a continuation does the
driver spawn a worker. The page channel has capacity one. The worker fetches then
sends, so in addition to the consumer's page and one queued page it can hold a
newly fetched page while waiting to send; this is not an exact one-page total
memory bound. Dropping the pager closes the receiver, and the worker stops when
its next send observes closure. It does not immediately cancel an already
in-flight fetch. Its page deadline still applies unless disabled.
The detached worker owns the state needed to finish that fetch, so request
metrics, history callbacks, and connection-level feedback can occur after the
pager has been dropped.

items.text:
A non-row success on the first page produces an empty stream, after required
keyspace or schema-change handling. A non-row response on a subsequent page is
an unexpected-response error. Later request failures are delivered through the
stream and stop the background fetching loop. Empty pages are skipped without
mistaking them for final completion. Cancellation of waiting for the next row
does not consume a row.

items.text:
The public typed stream yields owned values because its interface cannot return
values borrowing from a changing page. Conversion to a typed stream checks the
initial page's result types. Later pages are type-checked when their first raw row
is yielded, before typed decoding; empty pages are skipped without that check.
This permits detection of schema changes on pages containing rows. A type-check
or typed-value decoding error has already consumed that row. Raw row-framing
errors decrement the remaining-row count but can recur at the same malformed
bytes. These errors do not themselves stop the background worker; the caller can
continue polling. Manual/unpaged results can instead lend references into their
retained response bytes; see
[serialization/protocol](serialization-protocol.md).

the current page. Unlike a single-page result, the pager does not expose a
warnings collection; page processing discards response warnings.

checking and value-decoding errors.

items.text:
Row access supports an iterator, optional first row, required first row, and
exactly one row. The optional-first operation permits zero rows; required-first
rejects zero; exactly-one rejects both zero and multiple rows. These convenience
operations do not scan and validate all unused later row payloads. Column metadata
can be inspected by position or name; name lookup uses exact string equality
and returns the first matching column and its index when names repeat.
The result reports row count and encoded
row-byte size independently of decoding into application values.

Results, timestamps, and response side effects
items.text:
Timestamp precedence is an explicit statement/batch timestamp, then the session's
configured generator, otherwise no client timestamp. Timestamps are microseconds.
An explicit CQL timestamp clause has server-side precedence. No generator is
configured by default. A generated timestamp is obtained inside each connection
attempt, so retries, speculative branches, and pages can get different timestamps.
The internal unprepared-repair resend and repeated batch-repair sends reuse their
already constructed request timestamp. The simple generator uses wall-clock time
without monotonic guarantees and panics if time precedes the epoch. The monotonic
generator atomically chooses a greater wall-clock value or the preceding value
plus one; its guarantee is per generator instance, including concurrent callers.
It warns about clock drift exceeding one second at most once per second by
default, with configurable or disabled drift warnings. A wall clock before the
epoch also takes the increment path and emits a warning.

items.text:
A successful keyspace-change response causes session-wide keyspace propagation
before the public operation completes. A successful schema-change response, when
automatic agreement is enabled, waits for agreement including the response's
coordinator and then refreshes metadata if configured. Both options default to
enabled. The default agreement interval is 200 ms and its separate timeout is
60 seconds. A side-effect failure is returned even though the original database
operation may already have succeeded. This handling occurs after the core request
has logged its success and outside its request deadline; there is no automatic
retry of the original successful statement because side-effect handling failed.
The same first-response handling applies to automatic pagers. Exact agreement,
reachability, and keyspace-switch rules are in
[metadata/control/events](metadata-control-events.md) and [connections](connections.md).

items.text:
Tracing details are fetched separately by querying trace-session and trace-event
tables concurrently. These independent reads do not establish that every trace
event has arrived. An incomplete trace means no session row, missing duration,
or no events; that case is retried up to the configured attempt count, default ten,
with a default 3 ms interval. An incomplete attempt sleeps even when it is the
last configured attempt. Query errors return immediately. Row/type decoding
errors return when that result is inspected: event rows are inspected only after
a session row with a duration exists, so incomplete session data can defer
discovery of malformed event rows.
Default trace-fetch consistency is ONE. Exhausted incomplete attempts return an
empty-results error. Query history and metrics count the execution core's
requests/attempts; their full listener/reporting contract belongs to
[configuration/security/observability](configuration-security-observability.md).

section: Statements, execution, paging, retry, and speculation
items.text:
The stable API uses `Session::{query,execute}_{unpaged,single_page,iter}`,
`Session::execute_bound_*`, `Session::{prepare,prepare_batch,batch}`,
`PreparedStatement::bind`, `CachingSession`, `QueryResult`, `QueryRowsResult`, and
`QueryPager::rows_stream`. `PagingState::{start,as_bytes_slice,new_from_raw_bytes}`
supports manual continuation storage, while `PagingStateResponse::{finished,
into_paging_control_flow,new_from_raw_bytes}` represents completion independently.
`CachingSession::{add_prepared_statement,prepare_batch}` provides preparation
without execution. The deprecated public `QueryPager::type_check` checks only
the current page; it does not establish type compatibility for later pages.
`rows_stream` performs the required repeated checks. Custom `RetryPolicy`
implementations create branch-local `RetrySession` objects; although the trait
includes `reset`, this execution core creates fresh sessions instead of resetting
and reusing them across requests/pages.
The unified execution core also serves a fixed-connection
pager for internal metadata requests. That internal path uses one connection,
fallthrough retries, no speculation/metrics/history, a per-page timeout, and
requires row responses; its complete control-connection context is specified in
[metadata/control/events](metadata-control-events.md).

section: Statements, execution, paging, retry, and speculation
items.text:
Several preserialized-value and raw-result APIs are conditional wrapper-driver
interfaces, not general stable APIs: Python serialization/execution/raw result
access, C# preserialized paging/raw column iteration, C++ result decomposition,
and Node.js raw-row/metadata access require their respective unstable feature
gates and the unstable configuration.
Preserialized execution can bypass normal bind validation; raw result access
leaves row type checking/decoding to its caller. These interfaces have their own
contracts. In particular, Python's
[`Session::execute_unstable`](https://github.com/scylladb/scylla-rust-driver/blob/f8b0ee928dc0dcb475247dc82cce4e42804b0621/scylla/src/client/session.rs#L2048)
accepts already serialized values, a paging flag, and an input continuation.
With paging disabled it omits page size but still returns the response's
continuation, without the stable unpaged method's finished-state check.
Python also exposes `PreparedStatement::serialize_values_unstable` (which does
validate values), `QueryResult::deserialized_metadata_and_rows`, and the
`RequestInfo::new` constructor for retry-policy integration.
Specifically, [`QueryPager::next_column_iterator`](https://github.com/scylladb/scylla-rust-driver/blob/f8b0ee928dc0dcb475247dc82cce4e42804b0621/scylla/src/client/pager.rs#L748) is public only with both
`scylla_unstable` and `unstable-csharp-rs`. It is a cancellation-safe lending
operation returning a column iterator and a fresh-page flag; callers must check
each new page's types before typed decoding. See
[serialization/protocol](serialization-protocol.md) for this gated borrowing API.

items.text:
Database and proxy suites exercise statement behavior and inspect protocol traffic,
including recovery, retry decisions, page boundaries, and result metadata changes.
Tests using multiple nodes, Scylla extensions, or CCM need those environments;
their existence does not establish portability or a passing local run.
In particular, metadata-ID tests return early when that extension is absent;
`test_mixed_cluster` disables its advertisement on one proxy node rather than
running different server versions. The special-query metadata test starts a CCM
cluster with password authentication and authorization enabled. The large-batch
and CDC-partitioner tests are ignored under `cassandra_tests`, and the metrics
test module is compiled only with the `metrics` feature. The SELECT-without-FROM
test skips only on a `SyntaxError` from its initial capability probe; other errors
fail the test. Tracing integration helpers use 200 fetch attempts at 50 ms,
so they do not verify readiness with the production defaults of ten at 3 ms.

items.text:
For concurrency, race profile remapping with request creation; race cache misses
for equal and unequal strings; change keyspace while reusing unqualified cache
keys; update metadata from concurrent results; drop a pager before, during, and
after a background fetch. Verify actual node/shard and request bytes, not only
eventual success. Compare default and downgrading retry policies and check both
regular serial consistency and an ordinary consistency with a serial option.
The Rust implementation's limitations must stay visible when the Go design
deliberately improves them; improvements are not retroactive Rust guarantees.

The driver translates typed values and rows to CQL native-protocol requests and
exposes typed, dynamic, and partially decoded views of responses. It validates
the requested destination types against server metadata, distinguishes null,
unset, and zero-length values, and supports values borrowing the response frame.
This is a specification of the pinned Rust implementation, including its limits;
it is not a claim that all its encoding or decoding paths are zero-copy.

  only when the direction bit is set and the remaining version bits equal 4.
  It does not implement native-v5 segmented framing or negotiate a lower native
  version after rejection. Scylla extensions add specific capabilities to v4.

  opcode, and unsigned 32-bit body length, in network byte order. The stream is
  inserted after serialization, immediately before dispatch. Response opcodes are
  validated; unknown opcodes and wrong direction/version return parsing errors.

items.text:
- Client messages are STARTUP, OPTIONS, QUERY, PREPARE, EXECUTE, REGISTER, BATCH,
  and AUTH_RESPONSE. Responses are ERROR, READY, AUTHENTICATE, SUPPORTED, RESULT,
  EVENT, AUTH_CHALLENGE, and AUTH_SUCCESS. RESULT distinguishes VOID, ROWS,
  SET_KEYSPACE, PREPARED, and SCHEMA_CHANGE. Authentication conversation, event
  dispatch, and connection establishment are separate features.

items.text:
- A response body is read completely into owned memory before higher-level
  parsing. Early EOF and body/header I/O failures retain their parsing stage.
  The implementation currently has no explicit maximum incoming-frame-size
  guard before allocating for the advertised length. This is an observed limit,
  not a recommended acceptance rule for a new implementation. Outgoing frame
  construction casts the final body length to unsigned 32 bits without a checked
  conversion; individual cell limits do not establish a checked whole-frame limit.

items.text:
- Body flags identify compression, tracing, custom payload, and warnings. A
  compressed body without a configured compression algorithm is an error.
  After decompression, this implementation consumes tracing ID, then warnings,
  then custom payload, before leaving the main response body for its parser.
  The ordering here records the source implementation, not a generalized
  ordering rule for other protocol implementations.

- Unknown response-header flag bits are ignored. Response-body dispatch does
  not require full consumption: READY ignores its body, and VOID ignores bytes
  after the result-kind integer. Other ordinary response parsers likewise do
  not add a final end-of-body check. A successful parse therefore need not
  establish that every advertised body byte belongs to the decoded message.

items.text:
- Tracing IDs are UUIDs; warnings are owned strings; a response custom payload
  is a string-to-byte-buffer map. Outbound request construction exposes a tracing
  flag but does not expose a symmetric arbitrary outgoing custom-payload field.
  Decoding a response payload does not expose it on the ordinary query-result
  API: EXECUTE processing can consume tablet feedback from it, and conversion
  to a non-error query response discards the payload. Warning and tracing-ID
  retention differs between ordinary results, errors, and automatic paging;
  see [configuration and observability](configuration-security-observability.md).

items.text:
- LZ4 and Snappy operate on the frame body, leaving the header uncompressed.
  LZ4 prepends a four-byte big-endian uncompressed size to the compressed block.
  A shorter-than-four-byte LZ4 body is rejected before reading that size.
  Snappy uses its raw block format. Decompression produces a new owned buffer;
  borrowed result values subsequently refer to that decompressed buffer.
  The driver imposes no separate decompressed-size or expansion-ratio limit;
  the LZ4 size prefix is passed to the decompressor without such a bound.

items.text:
- OPTIONS/SUPPORTED and STARTUP establish per-connection extension support.
  Recognized numeric extension fields that are absent or fail to parse are
  treated as unsupported; the parser does not make them a connection error.
  It uses the first exact `KEY=` entry, so a malformed first value is not
  rescued by a later duplicate in that list. Before feature parsing, duplicate
  top-level SUPPORTED keys replace their entire earlier value list with the
  last wire entry. These are distinct duplicate-handling rules.
  Tablet-v1, tablet-v2, and metadata-ID support
  depend on key presence, even with an empty advertised value list.
  Extension support must not be inferred solely from the server product name.

- The rate-limit extension supplies a server-selected error code. The LWT
  metadata extension supplies a bit mask, and a prepared statement is marked as
  LWT only when all bits of that mask occur in its prepared-metadata flags.
  A negotiated zero mask therefore matches every prepared flag value; without
  negotiation, no LWT mark is inferred by this parser.

items.text:
- Tablet routing v2 supersedes v1: if the server advertises both, STARTUP enables
  only v2. Every EXECUTE on a v2 connection includes exactly one trailing tablet
  version-block byte after its ordinary query parameters. A non-v2 EXECUTE does
  not include or consume that byte. Block construction and response tablet hints
  belong to [routing](routing.md).

  contains a length-prefixed query string. AUTHENTICATE names the requested
  authenticator; challenge, success, and response tokens are optional byte
  strings whose contents belong to the authentication provider.

  aggregate targets also carry argument-type names. Unknown schema change kinds
  become an explicit Invalid value, while unknown schema target kinds fail.

- CLIENT_ROUTES_CHANGE currently accepts UPDATE_NODES. It carries paired lists
  of connection-ID strings and host-ID UUID strings; unequal counts and invalid

- The presence of an option controls its wire flag. A present but zero-length
  paging token is distinguishable from no token. Values are emitted in server
  bind-marker order. Named application values are reordered client-side; outgoing
  query serialization does not set the protocol named-values flag. The auxiliary
  request decoder rejects named-values frames as unsupported.

  flag bit; BATCH decoding accepts only its serial-consistency (`0x10`) and
  timestamp (`0x20`) flags and rejects any other bits.
  The low-level parameter codec writes any signed 32-bit page size verbatim;
  positive-page-size validation belongs to the higher-level statement API.

items.text:
- A value is framed by signed 32-bit length followed by its bytes. `-1` writes
  null, `-2` writes unset, and `0` writes a present zero-length value. Maximum
  ordinary cell payload is `2^31 - 1` bytes. The row/batch value count and batch
  statement count each fit an unsigned 16-bit integer. Collection counts fit a
  nonnegative signed 32-bit integer; overflow fails serialization.
  A low-level row writer can exceed 65,535 values; complete-row construction
  and batch serialization check the count after the row codec returns. The
  incremental `add_value` API checks that limit before invoking the cell codec.

  decoder rejects other kind bytes.

items.text:
- Single prepared executions serialize their values into owned row storage
  before awaiting execution; binding a prepared statement retains that storage
  for reuse. Complete request framing and compression also finish synchronously
  into an owned buffer before awaiting the router's submission queue. The queued
  bytes do not borrow application values. Dropping an async request cannot
  interrupt a synchronous codec invocation during its poll, and cancellation
  after submission does not revoke the router's buffer or guarantee server-side
  cancellation; stream cleanup is specified in [connections](connections.md).

items.text:
- Replayable batch-value providers can avoid constructing a separate collection
  of rows. Each traversal obtains a new iterator; the iterator-backed adapter
  does this by cloning its stored iterator, which should be inexpensive and
  reproduce the same values. Counting can consume an iterator, and each retry
  obtains another. Batch serialization invokes row codecs on each send, except
  that the session caches the row at statement index zero when that statement
  was already prepared and its value row exists. A prepared statement later in
  the batch, or preparing the first statement during a connection attempt,
  does not activate this cache. The driver does not pre-serialize and cache every
  batch row for retries. Batch routing uses the same first-statement boundary,
  as specified in [execution](execution.md#batches-and-their-routing-inputs).

section: Null, unset, empty, and omitted fields
items.text:
- Unset means a bound value is not supplied, and is represented separately from
  null, including an optional “set versus unset” wrapper. It is an outbound
  binding state, not a normal row-result value. The low-level request-value
  reader recognizes only `-1`, `-2`, or nonnegative lengths; more negative lengths
  fail. In contrast, the low-level response `[bytes]` reader treats *any* negative
  length as null. The spec must not claim stricter response validation than this.

section: Collections, vectors, dynamic values, and user codecs
items.text:
- A vector's dimension is an unsigned 16-bit metadata value; the custom-type
  parser accepts zero as well as 1 through 65,535. The wire value has
  no element-count prefix. Boolean, float, double, int, bigint, timestamp, UUID,
  and timeuuid elements use contiguous fixed-width encodings. A nested vector
  also uses fixed-width encoding when its own element type has a fixed vector
  width; its width is that element width multiplied by its dimension. Other
  native types (including tinyint, smallint, date, time, and inet), collections,
  tuples, UDTs, and vectors with variable-width elements use an unsigned
  variable-integer byte length before each encoded element.
  Nested fixed-width dimension products use unchecked platform-sized arithmetic;
  sufficiently large nested metadata can panic with overflow checks enabled or
  wrap without them. The unsigned-16-bit dimension limit does not bound the
  aggregate byte width. Fixed-width `nth` skip-size multiplication has the same
  unchecked-arithmetic boundary.

section: Collections, vectors, dynamic values, and user codecs
items.text:
- Serialization checks vector length equals its dimension. Fixed-width vector
  decoding can validate and process a contiguous run in bulk, then use ordinary
  element iteration for the remainder. A nonempty remainder shorter than the
  required element length fails; complete exhaustion is passed to the element
  decoder as null and may succeed for a nullable element destination. After a
  variable-length prefix, even a zero-length element is passed as null if no
  bytes remain, but as a present empty slice if later bytes remain. These are
  implementation quirks, not server validity guarantees. Errors distinguish
  element decoding from length/framing failures; the variable-width element
  error currently records the element type rather than the enclosing vector.
  Vector iteration is bounded by the metadata dimension. List/set/map iteration
  is bounded by the wire count; tuple and UDT decoding is bounded by metadata
  fields. These paths ignore surplus bytes after the expected elements/fields,
  even when the surplus is malformed. Ordinary row iterators likewise stop at
  the advertised row count without checking for surplus row bytes.

- Lazy list/set/map iteration is not terminated by an item error. A fully framed
  item whose value decoder fails has already been consumed, so later items can
  still decode. A map reads both key and value frames before decoding either;
  a value-framing failure therefore takes precedence over a key-decoding
  failure. A failed length-framed read leaves its bytes in place while consuming
  an expected-item slot, so continued iteration repeats a framing failure until
  the declared count is exhausted. Variable-width vectors differ: their length
  prefix is consumed separately and is not rolled back on a subsequent failure.
  Collected destination codecs stop at the first error and return no partial
  collection.

- The dynamic value representation supports every column type and retains UDT
  keyspace, name, and field names. It owns its variable-sized data. Dynamic UDT
  serialization requires matching keyspace/name, emits missing fields as null,
  rejects unknown source field names, and uses the lexicographically first
  unknown name in its error. It is distinct from generated structural UDT
  codecs, which match field layout rather than enforcing that dynamic name pair.

  value winning; the selected value is removed after its first matching metadata

  list/set/vector variants all delegate to the sequence encoder. Consequently
  these source variant names do not require the identically named destination:
  metadata selects the sequence layout, including the vector dimension check.

section: Result metadata, type checking, and ownership
items.text:
- NO_METADATA uses shared cached prepared-result metadata when available. With
  no cached metadata it creates empty metadata; it does not invent column types.
  If the server sends metadata despite a cache, the newly sent metadata wins.
  Malformed newly sent metadata fails parsing; this path does not fall back to
  the cache. Row-count parsing can also fail after metadata was decoded, and
  returns an error rather than a partially usable metadata/rows result.
  In the NO_METADATA branches, the received column count is not checked against
  the cached metadata; the empty fallback has zero columns even if a nonzero
  count was advertised. Subsequent row traversal uses the chosen column specs.
  With the empty fallback, raw and lending iterators can therefore yield the
  advertised number of empty rows without consuming or validating any row
  payload bytes, even when the advertised column count was positive. Typed
  destinations requiring columns fail their metadata type check; destinations
  accepting zero columns can succeed.
  METADATA_CHANGED together with NO_METADATA is rejected when metadata-ID
  negotiation makes that flag meaningful. PREPARED with paging state is rejected.

- A raw row iterator scans length prefixes to find the next row even if the
  caller does not decode every column. Its declared row-count hint remains
  exact even when items are errors. A framing failure retains consumption of
  earlier columns and leaves the cursor at the failing column; subsequent calls
  encounter that same failure until the declared row count is exhausted. Column
  error context may change because each later row scan starts at column zero.
  A typed value-decoding failure after a successful row scan does not prevent
  decoding the next row. The lending iterator follows the same scan behavior.
  Individual `FrameSlice::read_cql_bytes` and `read_n_bytes` calls preserve their
  cursor on failure; this is not a transaction over an entire row or compound
  parser. Neither laziness nor a successful metadata type check proves the
  remaining result body is valid before it has been traversed.

- The stable asynchronous paged row stream requires destination rows independent
  of both the page-buffer and metadata lifetimes. Shared-owner blobs qualify;
  ordinary borrowed text/blob fields do not. It type-checks the initial page

  page does not invalidate independently retained shared-owner values. The
  internal lending pager waits for a page before consuming a row, so cancellation
  while that wait is pending does not consume the next row. A separately gated
  public lending API exposes the row view and whether its page is fresh; callers
  of that API are responsible for checking destination types against each page.

Native varint constructors preserve the supplied bytes, and serialization sends
them unchanged. Equality and hashing normalize leading zero bytes, retaining a
zero sign byte when needed; empty bytes and all-zero byte sequences compare as

that varint representation and the exact scale, so numerically equal decimals
with different scales need not compare equal.

Database errors preserve the server reason and relevant structured fields:
syntax, invalid/configuration, already-exists, function failure, authentication,
unauthorized, unavailable, overloaded, bootstrapping, truncate, read/write timeout,
read/write failure, unprepared, server/protocol error, and negotiated rate-limit.
Unknown numeric error codes remain an “other” code. Read/write failures carry
counts/consistency and data-present or write-type details; unknown write types
remain strings. Rate-limit errors carry operation and coordinator-rejection
information. Policy consequences are specified in execution, not inferred by
the decoder. Standard database error codes are matched before the negotiated
rate-limit code, so a collision retains the standard error interpretation.
Malformed fields of a recognized database error produce a parsing error with
the error family and field name; they are not downgraded to an unknown-code
error. Unknown rate-limit operation bytes are preserved as an “other” operation.

items.text:
The implementation does not provide a blanket rejection guarantee for every
malformed frame: examples above include unbounded advertised frame lengths,
negative response lengths interpreted as null, count-bounded iterators that do
not require end-of-buffer, unchecked metadata size arithmetic, and server-deferred
scalar/collection constraints. Malformed custom type names can also make parsing
fail to terminate, as described in the Rust-specific parser facts below.
These observations must not be silently promoted to stronger Go requirements or
mistaken for an instruction to reproduce avoidable validation weaknesses.

items.text:
- The stable CQL types/traits live in `scylla-cql-core`; `scylla-cql` provides
  protocol/runtime-oriented support and re-exports. The main driver re-exports
  application-facing codecs, but some lower-level public APIs (for example
  `SerializedValues`, `RawBatchValues`, and raw request types) require using the
  CQL crates directly. `SerializeValue` and `SerializeRow` can be
  custom implemented; deserializers use `DeserializeValue<'frame, 'metadata>`
  and `DeserializeRow<'frame, 'metadata>` with separate lifetimes.

- Scalar mappings include `i8/i16/i32/i64`, `f32/f64`, `bool`, `String`/`&str`,
  `Vec<u8>`/`&[u8]`/`Bytes`, `IpAddr`, `Uuid`, `Counter`, `CqlDate`, `CqlTime`,
  `CqlTimestamp`, `CqlDuration`, `CqlTimeuuid`, and owned/borrowed decimal/varint
  wrappers. Blob encoding also supports `[u8; N]`. Encoding delegates through
  `&T`, `Box<T>`, `Arc<T>`, and `Cow<T>`. Decoding `Box<T>`/`Arc<T>` first decodes
  the inner value, then constructs its owning container; `Box<str>`/`Arc<str>` copy text
  into owned storage. `Cow<'frame, T>` decoding delegates to `&'frame T` and
  returns `Cow::Borrowed`, preserving the frame lifetime.

items.text:
- `FrameSliceWithMetadata` implements `DeserializeValue` for any column type
  and returns its optional raw cell slice plus the metadata reference without
  interpreting the payload. `Option<FrameSlice<'frame>>` also accepts any column
  type and returns the optional raw slice unchanged, without retaining metadata.
  `ColumnIterator` similarly implements
  `DeserializeRow` with an unconditional type check and returns itself. These
  public deferred-decoding destinations still require later type/byte validation
  when the caller chooses a concrete destination; `ColumnIterator::type_check`
  can check a destination against its remaining column specifications.
  The compatibility `scylla_cql::value::deser_cql_value` function decodes a
  present cell into owned `CqlValue` using a borrowed slice, and does not advance
  its `&mut &[u8]` argument despite that argument's mutable type.

items.text:
- `BatchValues` accepts homogeneous slices/vectors, heterogeneous tuples of one
  through sixteen rows, references, and `BatchValuesFromIterator`. Its iterator
  operations serialize, test emptiness, or skip the next row, each advancing it;
  `count` consumes the remaining iterator. `RawBatchValues` and its adapter pair
  such providers with metadata contexts for protocol use; the raw vector form
  accepts already serialized rows. `SerializedValues::from_closure` returns the
  built row plus the closure's auxiliary result, while `new_from_frame` validates
  and copies the count-prefixed request values and advances past them. Its raw
  iterator preserves null/unset/value, but assumes valid stored framing and can
  panic if a custom writer produced malformed bytes.

items.text:
- Optional feature flags add `chrono-04`, `time-03`, `num-bigint-03`,
  `num-bigint-04`, `bigdecimal-04`, `secrecy-08`, and `secrecy-10` adapters;
  `full-serialization` enables those adapters. The `serde` feature supplies
  external serde derives for value wrappers and consistency deserialization;
  these representations are explicitly outside semver guarantees, and are not
  the CQL wire codec. Separately gated unstable inter-driver APIs expose raw
  result metadata/rows: `QueryRowsResult::raw_rows_with_metadata` borrows them
  with `scylla_unstable` plus `unstable-nodejs-rs`;
  `QueryResult::deserialized_metadata_and_rows` returns an optional borrow with
  `scylla_unstable` plus `unstable-python-rs`. The latter feature also exposes
  individual vector-element serialization helpers. `scylla_unstable` plus
  `unstable-cpp-rs` exposes `QueryRowsResult::into_inner`, transferring metadata,
  raw rows, tracing ID, warnings, and optional coordinator, and publicly
  re-exports `DeserializedMetadataAndRawRows` from the main driver.
  `QueryPager::next_column_iterator`, gated by
  `scylla_unstable` plus `unstable-csharp-rs`, exposes the cancellation-safe
  lending pager described above, returning a column iterator and a fresh-page
  Boolean without performing a destination type check. These unstable APIs are
  not included in `full-serialization`. See [core Cargo features](https://github.com/scylladb/scylla-rust-driver/blob/f8b0ee928dc0dcb475247dc82cce4e42804b0621/scylla-cql-core/Cargo.toml#L23)
  and [lending pager wrapper](https://github.com/scylladb/scylla-rust-driver/blob/f8b0ee928dc0dcb475247dc82cce4e42804b0621/scylla/src/client/pager.rs#L748).
  Native `CqlTime` decoding and its range-checking helper are unconditional.
  `chrono` is also an unconditional dependency for diagnostic formatting, while
  the `chrono-04` feature enables its CQL adapters. A Rust 1.94.1 core build with
  `--no-default-features` succeeds; this does not establish every optional-feature
  combination (see the round-03 report).

items.text:
- The optional external type mappings are `chrono::NaiveDate`,
  `chrono::NaiveTime`, and `chrono::DateTime<Utc>`; `time::Date`, `time::Time`, and
  `time::OffsetDateTime`; `num_bigint::BigInt` from either supported version;
  and `bigdecimal::BigDecimal`. They map to date/time/timestamp, varint, and
  decimal respectively, with the conversion limits described above. Native
  varint/decimal wrappers also expose feature-gated conversions to/from those
  external number types; borrowed wrappers convert to external owned numbers.
  `secrecy-08` supports `Secret<T>` and `secrecy-10` supports `SecretBox<T>` with
  the required inner codec and zeroization bounds. Both expose the inner value
  to the ordinary CQL encoder and wrap decoded values. Secrecy 0.10 additionally
  decodes `SecretString` via `String` and `SecretSlice<T>` via `Vec<T>`; these are
  owned representations, and encoding writes ordinary bytes into the request.

items.text:
- All four derive macros accept `#[scylla(crate = path)]`, directing generated
  code to that crate's `_macro_internal` exports instead of the default `scylla`
  path. Their shared attributes are `flavor = "match_by_name"` (default) or
  `"enforce_order"`, `skip_name_checks`, `rename`, and `skip`. Both value derives
  accept `forbid_excess_udt_fields` and field-level `allow_missing`; only
  `SerializeRow` accepts `flatten`. `default_when_null` controls both deserialize
  derives and is accepted but ignored by both serialize derives, permitting
  those derives to coexist on one struct. These attributes have the behavioral
  restrictions in the generated-code section above.

items.text:
- `FrameSlice` stores a borrowed subslice and a reference to the original
  `Bytes`. Cloning/splitting it does not clone the original buffer owner.
  `to_bytes` creates a shared slice without copying only when that owner is
  present; `new_borrowed` uses the copy fallback. Small retained `Bytes` slices
  may consequently retain a much larger result-frame allocation.
  `split_at` panics for an out-of-range split; `chunks_exact` omits a trailing
  short remainder and panics for zero chunk size. `as_slice_mut` changes the
  slice cursor, not the immutable payload; callers must keep it within the
  original owner if later calling `to_bytes`, whose `slice_ref` requires that
  relationship.

items.text:
- Self-borrowed metadata keeps its backing `Bytes` in a `Yoke` container whose
  public references are bounded by the container borrow. Its internal `'static`
  parameter is not a public promise of permanent storage. Cached metadata uses
  immutable `Arc` ownership; the prepared statement's `ColumnSpecsGuard` retains
  a cache snapshot while it is inspected. Codec error wrappers similarly own
  `Arc`-shared payloads, requiring custom errors to be `Send + Sync + 'static`;
  their mutable downcast succeeds only with exclusive ownership of that payload.
  Public `TableSpec`, `ColumnSpec`, and `ColumnType` ownership conversions detach
  borrowed metadata. `TableSpec::into_owned` reuses already owned strings, while
  nested `ColumnType::into_owned` can rebuild boxes and UDT ownership even when
  already owned; metadata ownership promotion is not universally allocation-free.

items.text:
- `SerializedValues` owns an intermediate vector; `write_to_request` copies its
  bytes into the request buffer. Uncompressed frame construction reserves the
  exact body size when the request supplies it. Compression first creates a body
  buffer and then compressed output. Duration encoding allocates a temporary
  buffer; variable-width vector encoding allocates temporary element and length
  buffers. Numeric endian conversion is work even when it needs no heap buffer.
  These are explicit boundaries for a future Go zero-copy design.

items.text:
- Ordinary `CellValueBuilder` use reserves an invalid `-3` length until
  explicitly finished; `WrittenCellProof` establishes that the writer was
  completed. Correct use must call `finish`; merely abandoning a builder does
  not provide a valid cell. The public `CellWriter::new_without_size` and
  `make_sub_writer_without_size` paths omit the present-value length prefix,
  as needed for vector elements. `set_value` still checks its slice length,
  but a builder in this mode neither reserves `-3` nor checks total length on
  `finish`. Null and unset still write their four-byte sentinel even in this
  mode. Completion proofs do not certify the surrounding vector's layout.

items.text:
- Protocol clients can implement `SerializableRequest` with an opcode, body
  serializer, and optional exact size hint. `DeserializableRequest` is an
  auxiliary inspection/testing API, not the network response decoder. Its
  feature-aware entry point matters for `ExecuteV2`: the deprecated featureless
  decoder always expects a result-metadata ID and never consumes the tablet-v2
  byte, while the older `Execute` codec has neither extension. Public low-level
  request construction relies on callers to choose extension fields consistent
  with negotiation; the normal connection path does so automatically. These
  auxiliary decoders do not guarantee an error return for every truncated input:
  query-parameter flags and batch kind/statement-kind/flags use `Buf::get_u8`,
  which panics when the next byte is absent. The `Request` and `RequestV2`
  dispatchers only decode QUERY, EXECUTE, and BATCH; supplying another valid
  request opcode reaches `unimplemented!` and panics.

items.text:
- Standard type descriptors parse native IDs and recursively parse collections,
  UDTs, and tuples. Custom type ID zero invokes the Cassandra-style parser,
  including `VectorType`, `FrozenType`, and hex-encoded UDT names. It reports
  unknown custom names, bad parameter counts, malformed hex, and trailing
  characters, but not every malformed input terminates with an error. The
  fixed-arity parameter fallback counts an iterator that repeatedly yields
  errors without advancing at EOF; for example, `ListType(Int32Type` never
  finishes parsing. This affects the shared List/Set/Map/Frozen parameter path.
  The tuple path instead collects a fallible iterator and stops at its first
  error, so its unterminated-input test does not establish that shared path's
  termination.
  The current parser rejects trailing whitespace after a type expression;
  leading whitespace and whitespace inside complex expressions are accepted
  where its grammar consumes them. Empty or all-whitespace input instead
  produces the blob type. An optional hexadecimal number followed by `:` is
  validated as a platform-sized unsigned integer and then discarded before
  parsing the type name. It recognizes
  `DateType` as the driver's Date native type, an implementation detail distinct
  from assuming all external marshaller aliases are semantically identical.

items.text:
- The remaining cataloged `mod.rs` and `lib.rs` modules establish exports;
  `_macro_internal.rs` supplies generated-code plumbing, including
  column-by-column flattened row serialization. They do not
  create additional independent wire types. `macros_doctests.rs` checks derive
  examples and compile failures, `book_tests.rs` imports book examples spanning
  several feature sections, and `serde_tests.rs` checks feature forwarding.
  Test utility modules are harness support, not runtime behavior. Public
  response serializers such as `SchemaChangeEvent::serialize` and
  `ResultMetadata::serialize`/`Prepared::serialize` support proxy/test response
  construction; they do not add a normal client response-sending path. The test metadata type encoder
  does not support vectors and panics on that branch.

confirmed_claims: All-member admission before send, first complete routing key, canonical batch repair and conditional/unknown gating; actual timestamp/now/keyspace protocol effects.
Schema-independent recursive Clone and explicit Collect detach nested borrowed storage; retained descriptors do not pin reusable destinations.
Immutable recursively compiled bindings check null/empty children and retain value/state/lease/content guards without warm recursive type walks.
Span LZ4/Snappy never gather source or recopy final transform output, raw fallback retains original backing, independent decode/ratio and configured bounds reject before allocation.
Immediate layout scan and lazy checked children/terminal iterators with shared range index; no eager per-element descriptors or payload copies.
Descriptor validation, defensive fields/columns, wire conversion, identity/frozen comparison and DAG handling.
Tagged dynamic values, lazy aggregate validation, exact type/state checks and one shared pointer-owned row index with detached Clone.
Typed wrapping retains server code/message/details and context causes; hostile framing/type/counts return bounded staged errors rather than driver panics.
Publish-before-events, highest-generation bounded overflow marker/closure, disabled registration, isolated dispatch and shutdown joins.
Actual DecodeInto field addresses, reset and composed/custom-plan destination propagation; no Decode-then-whole-row assignment.

confirmed_claims: All-member admission before send, first complete routing key, canonical batch repair and conditional/unknown gating; actual timestamp/now/keyspace protocol effects.
Schema-independent recursive Clone and explicit Collect detach nested borrowed storage; retained descriptors do not pin reusable destinations.
Immutable recursively compiled bindings check null/empty children and retain value/state/lease/content guards without warm recursive type walks.
Span LZ4/Snappy never gather source or recopy final transform output, raw fallback retains original backing, independent decode/ratio and configured bounds reject before allocation.
Immediate layout scan and lazy checked children/terminal iterators with shared range index; no eager per-element descriptors or payload copies.
Descriptor validation, defensive fields/columns, wire conversion, identity/frozen comparison and DAG handling.
Tagged dynamic values, lazy aggregate validation, exact type/state checks and one shared pointer-owned row index with detached Clone.
Typed wrapping retains server code/message/details and context causes; hostile framing/type/counts return bounded staged errors rather than driver panics.
Publish-before-events, highest-generation bounded overflow marker/closure, disabled registration, isolated dispatch and shutdown joins.
Actual DecodeInto field addresses, reset and composed/custom-plan destination propagation; no Decode-then-whole-row assignment.
Stable independent page owners, released-view checks, old-page retention and survival across session close until advance.
Validated positive signed-int32 configured frame/decompressed bounds reach raw, v5, handshake, streaming and builtin output acquisition; headers/completion stay int64 on386.
Exact entry/revision/schema epoch and opaque-ID equality fences; changed/NO_METADATA/empty pages select matching retained plans without stale publication retry.
Physical tuple frames, omitted nullable suffixes, codec-selected Empty and explicit UDT identity/directional field evolution.
Named/positional physical-order accessors, duplicate markers/aliases, ignored-cell framing and compile-once concurrent mappings.
Golden bytes and malformed width/range/sign/float-bit/calendar/bignumber/text cases, retaining lease/type validation.
Present/null/unset/logical Empty framing, transactional rollback and exact scalar widths/domains; empty blob/text remain present.
Actual v1/v2/hint byte/original leader and ordered replicas, exact overlap/epochs, no-op sharing, saturation invalidation and nonblocking feedback.
Checked UTF8/ASCII constructors/chunks and borrowed text backing; invalid content is an error rather than constructor panic.
Detached driver-owned verified TLS, inherited per-host hooks/context/logical SNI, per-connection auth cleanup, actual client certificates/tickets/cloud.
Actual native envelopes retain canonical spans; accepted/queued writes join input lifetime, partial writes poison, stable request IDs reserve orphans until response/death.
Positive exact dimensions and native fixed/variable/nested layouts; wrong widths/counts/trailing bytes reject.

items.text:
A session starts from a configuration containing contact points and optional
policies. Contact points can be hostnames or explicit socket addresses; hostnames
without a port use 9042. Contact points bootstrap discovery rather than defining
the entire set of nodes. Their addresses are not passed through the address
translator. Configuring contact points appends them in caller order. Session
creation validates the configuration before generating its identity or opening
connections, establishes cluster state, and then applies the configured initial
keyspace before returning success. Discovery and pool readiness details are in
the metadata and connections sections.

items.text:
Hostname-resolution failures are logged and skipped if any contact address remains;
if none remains, session creation fails with the failed-hostname list. Each hostname
contributes all of its resolved addresses, duplicates are removed, and initial
connection candidates are shuffled rather than attempted in configuration order.
Hostname lookups run concurrently, but startup awaits the whole group before
trying candidates. With no DNS timeout, one unfinished lookup can therefore hold
up startup even when an explicit socket address is also configured.
The DNS timeout applies separately to each lookup. After a non-timeout error,
the resolver retries the original string paired with port 9042, even if that
string already included a port. This fallback receives a fresh timeout budget;
if it also fails, the original error is returned, even when the fallback timed
out. A first-lookup timeout skips the fallback. Thus the configured duration is
not a single deadline for the complete hostname-resolution operation.
A failed candidate handshake does not prevent trying another contact point. If an
initial handshake succeeds but metadata fetching fails, startup can proceed with
previously obtained metadata or dummy contact-point metadata and no retained control
connection; background repair then attempts to restore it. Successful session
creation therefore does not guarantee complete metadata or usable pools.

items.text:
The builder is reusable: building a session clones its configuration. Ordinary
configuration values are captured by the resulting session; supplied policy,
authentication, and TLS objects can be shared. A default execution-profile handle
is an intentional indirection that can change the profile used by already-created
sessions and statements. Two separately created handles to the same profile are
not the same remapping group. A request keeps the profile snapshot it acquired
across retries and speculative attempts. An automatic pager captures its settings
once for all pages; separate manual page calls acquire their profiles separately.
Remapping changes subsequent acquisition, not these existing snapshots. The
snapshot fixes the selected settings and policy objects, not mutable state inside
shared policies.

Socket options are applied before bind/connect. A configured receive/send size is
cast to an unsigned 32-bit size and passed to the socket API without a range
check. On platforms with a wider configuration integer, values above 2³²−1
lose their high bits; for example, 2³² reaches the socket API as zero. This is
truncation, not rejection or saturation, and OS adjustment is also possible.
Explicit zero differs from leaving the option unspecified. Linger is truncated
to whole seconds: zero and positive values below one second request reset-on-close;
values of at least one second request timed lingering. The TCP
keepalive setting means idle time before probes begin, not the interval between
probes. Where supported by the target OS, probes are one second apart and the
retry count is ten; the platform-specific branches do not promise identical
support on every OS. TCP keepalive is separate from CQL OPTIONS keepalive.

The built-in username/password provider emits a zero byte, UTF-8 username, another
zero byte, and UTF-8 password. It does not select behavior based on the advertised
authenticator name. It accepts the success phase without interpreting its token
and rejects any challenge. Configuring this provider does not enable TLS; transport
encryption is a separate choice. A custom provider can implement challenge-based
authentication and is shared safely across simultaneous connection handshakes,
while each exchange has its own mutable state. The driver does not serialize calls
to a shared provider; within one exchange, it awaits each challenge handler before
proceeding. The success handler runs only for AUTH_SUCCESS. A failed or cancelled
handshake can drop its exchange without calling that handler; it is not a general
cleanup notification.

dangerous because the underlying raw builder does not enable verification by
